anonymous-sources-bodies-came-from-a-sub: A podcast host, Jesse Michels, has looked into small three-fingered bodies reported from the Nazca region of Peru in recent years. He says several anonymous sources told him the bodies really come from a large tunnel system underground. If so, it would point to where they came from and that more might be down there.
anonymous-usaf-colonel-and-fighter-pilot: A filmmaker who makes documentaries about UFOs, James Fox, says he knows a colonel and fighter pilot in the US Air Force, whom he does not name. Fox says this man told him he had a very dramatic UFO encounter around 1980, the kind of account that matters because it comes from a trained military flyer.
anonymous-whistleblower-on-crash-retriev: A longtime UFO disclosure campaigner, Steven Greer, relays the story of an unnamed insider who came to him. Greer says this man was on a crash retrieval team, a group sent to recover crashed objects, working far north in the Nevada desert on land once called the Nevada Test Range, and that around 2009 his team was retrieving these objects. If true, it would mean such recoveries were still happening in recent years.
another-aerospace-company-leaves-the-wor: A physicist, Eric Davis, says that a senior vice president of an aerospace company, one he does not name, told him about secret work on studying and copying unknown technology. As Davis recalls it, that company more or less walked away from the whole line of work in the early 1970s, which would mean such programmes once ran inside private industry and some firms dropped out.
another-channeler-also-predicted-the-cha: A psychology researcher and interviewer, Jeffrey Mishlove, says that in the San Francisco Bay Area a channeler, someone who claims to pass on messages from spirits or other beings, foretold the 1986 Challenger disaster, when a NASA space shuttle broke apart after launch. He says that afterwards he heard from people at the Foundation for Mind Being Research, a local group, that they knew of another channeler who had made the same prediction. If true, it would suggest such people can sense future events.
antarctica-as-the-nordics-main-subterran: A researcher named Jason Jorjani, speaking in 2025 on podcast host Jesse Michels's show, talks about a group of beings he calls the Nordics, whom he had discussed in an earlier interview. He says their main hidden base, underground and reached by submarine, is in Antarctica. If true, non-human beings would be living in secret at the bottom of the world today.
anthony-hopkins-finds-feifer-s-annotated: A well-known skeptic and writer, Michael Shermer, retells a famous coincidence about the actor Anthony Hopkins and a novel called The Girl from Petrovka by the author George Feifer. As Shermer tells it, around 1972 Hopkins was heading home and happened upon a copy of the book on a bench at Leicester Square tube station in London, and it turned out to be Feifer's own copy with his notes in it. The story is told to show how strange coincidences can feel meaningful.
anti-drone-technology-fails-at-pseg-sale: A researcher who has long studied UFO sightings at nuclear sites, Robert Hastings, says an unnamed person who could see the internal messages of the Salem and Hope Creek nuclear power plants in New Jersey, run by the utility PSEG, told him about events in 2024. According to that source, several drones were seen over the plant, staff tried to use anti-drone equipment that normally works on any drone, and it failed completely. If true, the objects would be something beyond ordinary drones.
anti-gravity-researcher-amy-eskridge-and: A podcast host, Jesse Michels, tells of Amy Eskridge, a researcher into anti-gravity, meaning ways to cancel or push against gravity, who he says died in 2022 under very mysterious circumstances. According to Michels, near the end of her life she kept talking about a sixth force, an unknown force of nature beyond the known ones. In another telling he says people were attacking her with directed energy, beams of energy used as a weapon, leaving burns on her hands, and he also mentions her father Richard. If true, it would mean her work was seen as dangerous enough to target her.
antikythera-mechanism: A podcast host, Jesse Michels, describes the Antikythera mechanism, an ancient device found in a shipwreck in the Aegean Sea, the stretch of water between Greece and Turkey. He calls it almost an astronomically aligned computer, which, as he tells it, would show that ancient people had far more advanced knowledge than we assume.
anton-bilton-s-proposed-dmt-telepathy-ex: A podcast host, Jesse Michels, tells of a man named Anton Bilton who was thinking of giving people DMT, a powerful psychedelic drug, and placing them in side-by-side Faraday cages, metal enclosures that block radio and electrical signals. The idea was to test whether they could share thoughts with no ordinary signal passing between them, which would point to telepathy.
antonio-villas-boas-has-intercourse-with: A researcher named Mike Masters, on Jesse Michels's podcast, tells of Antonio Villas Boas, a man in Brazil who in 1957 says he had physical intercourse with a woman aboard a craft. According to Masters, Villas Boas described her as a woman who looked slightly different from women he knew, with higher cheekbones and a pointier chin. Masters raises it because, if true, it would suggest the visitors are close enough to humans to be related to us.
anunnaki-came-to-earth-to-mine-gold: Geoffrey Drumm, a man who talks about the true purpose of the Egyptian pyramids, retells on podcast host Jesse Michels's show the story of the Anunnaki, beings from ancient Middle Eastern myth. According to Drumm, they came to Earth long ago to mine gold and other precious metals. If true, humanity's distant past would have been shaped by visitors who came here for resources.
apollo-11-crew-observes-a-glowing-arista: A researcher who appeared as a guest on a podcast says that during Apollo 11, the 1969 mission that first landed people on the Moon, astronomers in Germany saw Aristarchus, a crater on the Moon, shining unusually bright. The guest ties this to the crew, Neil Armstrong, Buzz Aldrin and Michael Collins, being asked to look at the glowing crater, which would hint at something odd happening on the Moon.
apollo-11-halfway-to-the-moon-window-foo: A podcast host, Joe Rogan, points to footage that he says Bart Sibrel, a filmmaker who questions the moon landings, has uncovered from the 1969 Apollo 11 mission, the first crewed landing on the moon. As Rogan tells it, the footage shows the crew, including Neil Armstrong, saying they are far out in space, about halfway to the moon, while the claim is that they were really still circling close to Earth and faking the view through the window. If true, it would mean at least part of the famous journey was staged.
apollo-11-post-flight-press-conference-l: A popular podcast host, Joe Rogan, urges people to watch the press conference the Apollo 11 astronauts gave after returning from the first Moon landing in 1969. He says it looks like a hostage video, and he cites an unnamed body language expert who reads the astronauts as hiding something, which would mean the public was not told everything about the trip.
apollo-11-timing-trinity-anniversary-and: A podcast host, Jesse Michels, points out that Apollo 11, the NASA mission that first landed people on the Moon, launched on July 16, 1969. According to Michels, that was exactly 24 years after Trinity, the first atomic bomb test, which he calls the dawn of the nuclear age. He sees the date as chosen on purpose, a hint that symbolic or ritual meaning shaped the space program.
apollo-11-trio-of-lights-frame-1969: Maaneli Derakhshani, speaking on Jesse Michels's podcast, says that a trio of lights seen in photographs from Apollo 17, a later NASA mission to the Moon, also shows up in footage from Apollo 11, the 1969 mission that first landed people on the Moon. He points to the repetition across missions as a sign that something unexplained was there, rather than a one-off flaw in a single picture.
apollo-11-watched-by-craft-on-the-moon-a: A man named Steve Coburn, speaking on a podcast, repeats a story about Apollo 11, the 1969 NASA mission that first put people on the Moon. He says whistleblowers at NASA, the US space agency, claimed astronaut Neil Armstrong talked on a private radio channel after landing, and the story holds that unknown craft watched the crew on the Moon and followed them on the way. If true, the astronauts were not alone up there.
apollo-13-zapped-because-of-a-nuclear-de: A man named Steve Coburn told podcast host Jesse Michels that he learned Apollo 13, the American Moon mission of 1970 that went wrong, may not have failed because of a mechanical fault. He says it may have been zapped by aliens because it may have carried a nuclear warhead, and he points to the Atomic Energy Commission, the US agency that oversaw nuclear matters. If true, it would mean aliens actively stop nuclear weapons from going into space.
apollo-14-blue-orb-above-mitchell-blacke: A researcher, Maaneli Derakhshani, says that in a photo from Apollo 14, the 1971 moon landing mission, a blue orb can be seen very clearly in the lunar sky above the astronaut Edgar Mitchell. He says the orb shows up in one archive of the mission photos but is blacked out in the scan held by the Lunar and Planetary Institute, a research centre that keeps NASA's moon images. If true, it would mean something unexplained was on the moon with the astronauts and that the record was later edited.
apollo-17-insectoid-metallic-probe-in-lu: A guest on a podcast, Maaneli Derakhshani, says that among NASA's public photos from Apollo 17, the 1972 Moon mission flown by astronauts Eugene Cernan and Harrison Schmitt, there is an image with something in the lunar sky. He says that if you brighten the picture, it looks like an insect-shaped probe, a bluish metal object, which would suggest something artificial was near the astronauts on the Moon.
apollo-17-trio-of-blue-lights-1972: A researcher named Maaneli Derakhshani, speaking on podcast host Jesse Michels's show, describes a sighting from Apollo 17, a 1972 Moon landing mission run by NASA, the US space agency. He says a raw scan of a photo frame from the mission shows "three solidish looking blue lights", spaced almost evenly apart in a small patch of the lunar sky above the landing site. He tells it because, if it holds up, something unexplained would have been photographed on the Moon.
apollo-8-launched-on-the-winter-solstice: A podcast host, Jesse Michels, notes that Apollo 8, the NASA mission that first flew astronauts around the Moon, launched on December 21, 1968. That was the winter solstice, the longest night of the year, when the sun is symbolically reborn. He tells it as a sign that NASA timed its launches around old pagan, sun-centred symbolism.
apollo-astronauts-given-suicide-pills-19: A documentary filmmaker named James Fox, on Jesse Michels's podcast, passes on what a woman named Fay Ann Potter told him about the 1969 Moon missions run by NASA, the US space agency. According to her, NASA officials said the astronauts were each given a pill that would kill them if anything went wrong. He tells it as a sign of how much was kept hidden about those missions.
apollo-crew-followed-by-something-to-the: Apollo 11 was the 1969 NASA mission that first landed people on the Moon. A documentary filmmaker named James Fox says that Fay Ann Potter, the sister of astronaut Buzz Aldrin, told him Aldrin had said the crew was followed by something on the way to the Moon. In a later telling, Fox puts it as Aldrin having had a UFO encounter of his own during the trip. A podcast host, Jesse Michels, says Aldrin admitted openly in several interviews that something was following them. If true, it would mean the first Moon crew had company.
apollo-intersecting-shadows-suggest-mult: A podcast host, Joe Rogan, speaking on Jesse Michels's show, points to the crossing shadows in photos from the Apollo Moon missions of 1969. He says people like to try to dismiss them, and the story goes that shadows falling in different directions mean more than one light source, which, if true, would raise doubts about how the photos were made.
apollo-lunar-dust-in-charles-s-lab-and-l: A NASA scientist named Charles tells podcast host Jesse Michels that he keeps about 200 grams of Moon dust in his lab, brought back by the Apollo missions that landed astronauts on the Moon between 1969 and 1972. He also talks about retroreflectors, mirrors left on the Moon's surface that bounce lasers back to Earth, including a recent one carried by a newer lander.
apollo-lunar-photo-lights-and-buzz-aldri: During the Apollo Moon missions, some photos show small blue lights in the sky, and astronaut Buzz Aldrin reported seeing flashes of light inside the cabin. A skeptic writer named Michael Shermer says an astronomer, Avi Loeb, explains both as cosmic rays, fast particles from space hitting the camera or the eye, and Shermer thinks he is right. A guest named Maaneli Derakhshani also credits Loeb, but ties the idea only to a trio of blue lights in photos from Apollo 17, a later mission. A podcast host, Jesse Michels, says instead that the astrophysicist Neil deGrasse Tyson put the Apollo 17 lights down to cosmic rays and called it case closed. The point of the explanation is that the lights would then need no unusual cause.
apollo-telemetry-data-and-original-foota: A podcast host, Joe Rogan, speaking on another host's show, talks about the Apollo missions, NASA's flights to the Moon around 1969. Rogan says that all the telemetry data, the stream of measurements sent back from the spacecraft, was destroyed along with original footage, and he calls that crazy. If true, it would mean key records of the Moon landings no longer exist.
aquarius-document-analyses-benowitz-film: An author named Greg Bishop says that around 1981, near Kirtland Air Force Base in Albuquerque, New Mexico, a UFO researcher named Bill Moore gave a man named Paul Bennewitz a paper known as the Aquarius document, which discussed films Bennewitz had made. Bishop says the paper mentioned access being limited to "MJ12," the first time anyone had used that name, and he calls the document fake, a story that matters because it would mean Bennewitz was being fed false material.
aquinas-s-mystical-experience-at-mass: A podcast host, Jesse Michels, says that Thomas Aquinas, a medieval Christian thinker, was working on his Summa Theologica, a huge book explaining God through reason, when he had a sudden conversion-like experience during mass. Michels tells it as an example of a deeply rational mind being overtaken by a direct mystical experience.
aquino-and-phoenix-program-psychological: A writer and researcher named Peter Levenda, on Jesse Michels's podcast, says that a man named Michael Aquino served as a psychological warfare officer during the Vietnam War. Levenda says Aquino was part of the Phoenix program, a wartime operation in Vietnam, and he draws on his own book, The Lovecraft Code, for the story. He raises it to link military mind-influence work with the wider themes of his research.
archaeological-retrieval-of-craft-from-t: Matthew Brown, a man presented on a podcast as a Pentagon whistleblower, talks about pulling craft up from the ocean floor as if it were an archaeological dig. Speaking with podcast host Jesse Michels, he says that anything buried under tens of meters of seabed sediment must have been there a very long time, because that much sediment takes ages to build up. If true, it would mean such craft have been on Earth for a very long time.
archaeologist-who-excavated-amenemhat-ii: A researcher who calls himself Luke Caverns talks about the pyramid of Amenemhat III, an Egyptian king who ruled around 1900 BC. He says the archaeologist who dug it out in the late 1800s, a man whose name he recalls starting with P, claimed it was never a real tomb but a symbolic one for the king's ka, the ancient Egyptian idea of a person's spirit or life force. That would mean at least some pyramids were not built as burial places.
archive-research-nixon-could-slip-his-se: A UFO researcher named Grant Cameron says people used to claim Richard Nixon, US president from 1969 to 1974, could never get away from his security guards. Cameron says he checked Nixon's records at the National Archives, where the US government keeps its official papers, and found Nixon slipped his security many times, including around his Florida home at Key Biscayne. That would leave room for the stories of him going places unseen.
archuleta-reports-a-crashed-plane-to-the: A researcher named Scott Ramsay, on a podcast episode about a reported crash with alien bodies in New Mexico, retells what a rancher named Valentine Archuleta did in March 1948. According to Ramsay, Archuleta called the Air Force, linked to Kirtland Air Force Base near Albuquerque, and said one of their planes had crashed on his land and they needed to come get it. The call is told as the start of the crash story.
area-51-barely-discussed-before-lazar-19: Area 51 is a secret military site in the Nevada desert, and a podcast host named Jesse Michels says that before 1989 almost nobody talked about it. In his telling, that changed when a man named Bob Lazar came forward, which would make Lazar the person who first put the base in the public eye.
area-51-caller-extradimensional-beings-c: In 1997 a caller to Coast to Coast AM, a late-night US radio show about the paranormal hosted by Art Bell, said he had worked at Area 51, a secret US military test site in Nevada. The caller said that what we think of as aliens are really beings from other dimensions, contacted by an early forerunner of the space program. The call was revisited on Jesse Michels' podcast with the musician Flying Lotus, and if true it would mean the government made contact long ago.
area-51-confirmed-under-the-obama-admini: Joe Rogan, a well-known podcast host, says on Jesse Michels's show that Area 51, a secret US military base in the Nevada desert long tied to UFO stories, was not officially admitted to exist until the Obama administration, sometime between 2009 and 2017. According to Rogan, that happened because the government wanted to widen the restricted zone around the site. He tells it to show how long the government kept even the base's existence quiet.
area-51-crash-either-secret-us-testing-o: A man named Ralph Larson, on an episode where he is presented as a former CIA chief, talks about a crash said to be linked to Area 51, a secret US military test site in the Nevada desert. Picking up an idea from the host, Jesse Michels, and admitting he has not researched it himself, he says it was either secret American testing or some intelligence watching the nuclear bomb tests nearby in the 1940s and 50s.
area-51-equipment-acquired-from-other-go: John Harrington, presented as a former US Secretary of Energy, says that there is equipment at Area 51, a secret military test site in Nevada, that the US acquired from other governments. He gives this as a reason the site is kept so closely guarded.
area-51-programs-moved-to-dugway-proving: An online researcher who goes by UAPGerb says Steven Greer, a well-known UFO campaigner, often claims that 35 to 40 percent of the secret projects at Area 51, the hidden Nevada test site, were moved to Dugway Proving Ground, an Army testing range in Utah. UAPGerb says a witness known only as AH said exactly the same thing in testimony recorded in 2000 and kept in an archive of such interviews. If so, Utah would be the new Area 51.
area-51-sensor-program-for-detecting-ufo: A podcast host, Jesse Michels, refers to The Age of Disclosure, a documentary film about UFOs. He says it was stated publicly in that film that at Area 51, a secret US military site in Nevada, there was some kind of sensor programme used to look for UFOs. If true, it would mean the government was actively watching for such objects there.
area-51-was-only-groom-lake-dreamland-wa: A man named Charles Hall, who told podcast host Jesse Michels he spent three years with tall white aliens at Nevada's secret test ranges, says that around 1965 the layout was different from what people assume. According to Hall, Area 51, the famous secret military base, was only the site at Groom Lake, a dry lakebed, while the real 'Dreamland,' the nickname for the most secret zone, was Areas 53 and 54. If true, it would mean the most hidden activity happened somewhere other than the well-known base.
area-51-workers-sickened-by-burning-haza: A scientist named John Brandenburg says workers at Area 51, the secret Nevada test site, got sick from hazardous waste being burned there and went to court. He says one man had to photograph the site from the highway and show a federal judge the buildings where he had worked, and the government's lawyers denied seeing any buildings in the pictures. He tells it to show how far the government would go to deny the base exists.
area-6-lockheed-martin-aerial-operations: A commentator who goes by the online name UAPGerb says, on Jesse Michels's podcast, that Area 6, a zone near Yucca Flat in the Nevada desert, holds an aerial operations facility owned by Lockheed Martin, a large American aerospace and defence company. He raises it while describing how the Pentagon's secret programme on unidentified craft is said to work, suggesting the site may play a part in it.
ariel-school-girl-to-john-mack-in-space-: Podcast host Jesse Michels often retells a moment from the Ariel School case, a 1994 event at a school in Ruwa, Zimbabwe, where children said they saw visitors from a craft. A Harvard psychiatrist named John Mack later interviewed the children, and Michels says one girl told him, "In space there's no love, but down here there is." In one telling Mack was asking how the beings spoke to the children by thought, and in another he was asking why the visitors had come. Michels shares it because, if true, it hints at why such beings might be interested in Earth.
ariel-school-landing-near-a-uranium-mine: In 1994, at the Ariel School in Ruwa, Zimbabwe, a group of schoolchildren said they saw a silver craft come down from the sky and land in a field near their school. A podcast host, Jesse Michels, puts the number at 62 and points out that a uranium mine was nearby. If true, a craft landed in front of children close to a source of nuclear material. David Grusch, a man who speaks publicly about secret UFO programs, says about 100 children saw walking, human-like beings he calls NHI, short for non-human intelligence. A man named Karl Nell says beings showed themselves to the children in the middle of the day. A filmmaker, James Fox, says he investigated it himself for a work called The Phenomenon and calls it an alleged landing seen by about 66 children, and he stresses the message the children say they received: "you don't understand how special you are." Others add details: one speaker, Merrick, says the children's drawings were identical, while a writer, Peter Levenda, says their stories do not always match. The tellers disagree on the number of children and on whether beings were seen.
ariel-school-witnesses-reunite-in-los-an: James Fox, a documentary filmmaker who investigates UFOs, tells podcast host Jesse Michels about the Ariel School case, in which a group of schoolchildren in Ruwa, Zimbabwe said they saw a craft land near their school. He says that in 2013, about twenty years later, the former pupils agreed for the first time to get back together, meeting in Los Angeles, which matters because it let the witnesses retell their story as adults.
aristotle-s-passage-on-the-ancestors-bel: James Madden, a guest on Jesse Michels's podcast, recalls a passage by Aristotle, the ancient Greek philosopher. According to Madden, Aristotle says this shows that our most ancient ancestors were not wrong when they believed there was a divinity surrounding nature. Madden brings it up to suggest that very old beliefs in intelligent powers around us may have been on to something.
aristotle-the-planets-are-intelligences: James Madden, speaking on Jesse Michels's podcast, says that for Aristotle, the ancient Greek philosopher, the planets were literally intelligences, living minds. He adds that they were not flying ships or anything like that. He uses the idea to suggest that ancient thinkers saw intelligence in the heavens without picturing it as machinery.
ark-moved-from-axum-to-lake-ziway-during: A writer on lost ancient civilisations, Graham Hancock, says the Ethiopians tell of the Ark of the Covenant, the sacred chest from the Bible, being moved when Italy occupied Ethiopia between 1935 and 1941. According to them, it was taken out of Axum, a holy city in the north, to an island on Lake Ziway for safekeeping. The story matters because it says where the Ark was kept.
ark-of-the-covenant-as-a-device-that-str: The Ark of the Covenant is the sacred chest that, in the Bible, the Israelites carried through the desert under Moses. A writer on ancient mysteries, Graham Hancock, points out on Jesse Michels's podcast that according to the Book of Exodus and other biblical passages, the Ark could also strike people dead with bolts of fire coming out of it. He tells it to suggest the Ark may have been some kind of powerful device rather than only a holy box.
ark-of-the-covenant-claimed-kept-at-aksu: An author named Graham Hancock says that while researching his book The Sign and the Seal, from the 1980s into the 1990s, he was told in the Ethiopian town of Aksum that the Ark of the Covenant, the sacred chest of the Bible, was kept there in a chapel beside the Church of St Mary of Zion. He recalls being told plainly, "we have the Ark of the Covenant here," which, if true, would place one of history's most famous lost objects in Ethiopia.
arkani-hamed-s-positive-geometries-outsi: Donald Hoffman, a scientist who studies perception, says on Jesse Michels's podcast in 2026 that physicists such as Nima Arkani-Hamed, at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, a research centre, are finding what they call positive geometries, mathematical structures that lie outside space and time. Hoffman calls Arkani-Hamed one of the first pioneers of this work. If he is right, space and time would not be the deepest layer of reality, leaving room for things we normally cannot perceive.
armageddon-as-a-kinetic-war-against-the-: A filmmaker and researcher named Tim Alberino, maker of a film called Birthright, tells podcast host Jesse Michels his reading of Armageddon, the final battle described in the Bible. Alberino says it is a war against the Son of God as he returns to Earth, and that he believes it will be a real, physical war fought with weapons. For him this would mean the end times are a literal conflict, not only a spiritual one.
armageddon-dream-with-the-number-747-and: A former CIA officer named Rolf Mowatt-Larssen says that in 1976, while at Fort Knox, an Army base in Kentucky, he had an incredibly vivid dream of fighting in a battle like Armageddon, the final battle at the end of the world. He says the dream featured the number 747 and cubes with numbers on them, and he tells it as one of the experiences that led him to wonder whether he could glimpse the future.
armed-trespasser-on-grillmair-s-property: A podcast host, Jesse Michels, in an episode about American scientists who he says have been going missing, tells of a scientist named Carl Grillmair. Citing sheriff's officials, court records and the Los Angeles Times, he says that on December 20, 2025, Grillmair called the police to report an armed person trespassing on his large property in Llano, California, and a name, Freddy Snyder, comes up in the account. Michels raises it as part of a pattern of threats around these scientists.
army-adapting-nhi-derived-electro-optic-: A researcher who goes by UAPGerb says on Jesse Michels's podcast that in the early 2000s the US Army wanted to fit electro-optic cloaking, a technology that hides objects from sight using light and electronics, onto its next generation of combat vehicles. In this story the technology is said to come from non-human intelligence, meaning beings that are not human. If true, it would mean such technology was being turned into military hardware.
army-interplanetary-phenomenon-unit-conf: A researcher who goes by UAPGerb tells podcast host Jesse Michels about the Interplanetary Phenomenon Unit, which he describes as a US Army group that dealt with UFO matters from 1947 to 1950. He says its existence was first confirmed in 1986 to a UFO researcher named William Steinman, and he points to a report and a field order from the unit. If true, it would mean the Army ran its own early UFO effort.
army-money-continues-after-the-round-tab: A researcher named Greg Malatzi, on Jesse Michels's podcast, talks about a 1957 group in Maine called the Round Table, linked in the episode to a scientist said to have contacted an alien council. Malatzi says that even after the group closed, its leader kept getting money from the US Army, and that records show this. If true, it would mean the military was quietly backing contact work.
army-officers-visiting-the-utah-ranch-fo: A ranch in Utah, known as Skinwalker Ranch, is said to be a place of strange happenings, and people who visited in the 1990s and 2000s say those happenings followed them home. A researcher, Jacques Vallee, says trained army officers spent a few days there, went home, and found some phenomenon following them. A podcast host, Jesse Michels, tells it more broadly of researchers studying the ranch, including people working for the businessman Robert Bigelow and a man named Jake Barber, who say they had to rid themselves of it. If true, it would suggest the phenomenon is not tied to one place but can attach to people.
army-public-affairs-source-terrified-of-: A UFO researcher who goes by the online name UAPGerb told podcast host Jesse Michels about a man he spoke with who worked in the US Army's public affairs office, the part of the Army that deals with the press and the public, in the mid-2010s. According to UAPGerb, this man said he was not really afraid of the CIA, the US spy agency, but was terrified of the NSA, the agency that intercepts and monitors communications. UAPGerb tells it as a hint that people near these secrets feel the eavesdroppers are the ones to fear most.
army-r-d-golden-age-and-institutions-to-: A UFO researcher who goes by the online name UAPGerb told podcast host Jesse Michels that the 1960s were a golden age of US Army research and development, at the time a man named Philip Corso was involved, alongside a man named Arthur Trudeau. UAPGerb says Corso claimed that institutions were also set up then to study technology from beings not from Earth, and he points to Army research primers, booklets from that time, as backing for the period. If true, it would mean the Army was quietly studying alien technology decades ago.
army-research-laboratory-finds-lifter-th: Gary McKinnon, a British computer hacker who says he found signs of a secret NASA space programme, talks on podcast host Jesse Michels's show about "lifters", light devices that rise when high voltage runs through them. He says the Army Research Laboratory, a US Army science lab, found sometime in the 2000s that their push was at least 10 to 20 percent stronger than the flow of electrically charged air, called ion flow, could explain. He also points to a group called Blaze Labs. If that is so, some force beyond ordinary airflow would be lifting them.
army-trucks-cordoning-off-the-hospital-1: In January 1996, in the Brazilian town of Varginha, many people say a strange craft came down and a living non-human creature was caught and taken to local hospitals. A surgeon named Italo Venturelli says he saw army trucks with green canvas covers lined up at the entrance of the town's Regional Hospital. If true, it would point to the military quietly handling something at the hospital that week.
arranging-and-conducting-the-bobby-ray-i: Jay Anderson, a man who interviews people about UFOs, says that in the 2020s he set up and recorded an interview with a man named Bobby Ray Inman. Anderson says Inman was relaxed until the talk turned to UFOs, and then, even when Anderson was only asking questions, things got tense. To Anderson, that shift suggests the subject touches something Inman would rather not discuss.
arrest-by-national-high-tech-crime-unit-: Gary McKinnon, a British computer hacker who says he found signs of a secret space program while breaking into NASA computers, says he was arrested in London around 2002. He recalls an officer named Jeff Donsson, from a British police unit for computer crime called the National High-Tech Crime Unit, telling him he was under arrest for computer misuse. It is the moment his hacking, which he links to hidden space secrets, caught up with him.
arrest-of-supervisor-and-100-million-abu: Jordan Jose is a man who says he was taken into a secret UFO programme as a child. Speaking with the podcast host Jesse Michels, he talks about a care facility called Baker Victory Services in Western New York, which he links to his story. He says a news article reports that a supervisor there was arrested on about 210 felony charges for altering records. He also says a $100 million lawsuit was settled over many years of sexual abuse claims. He raises this because, if true, it would show the place had something to hide. Later in the same interview he says the facility was sued so many times by other people, not by him, that it had to close. In that version he does not mention the arrest or the settlement.
arriving-gods-will-be-received-as-saviou: A filmmaker and researcher named Tim Alberino, who made a film called Birthright, tells podcast host Jesse Michels that a group of beings will one day arrive on Earth and be welcomed as the gods returning. Drawing on the Book of Revelation, the last book of the Bible, he links this arrival to the road toward Armageddon, the final battle. In his view it would mean humanity mistakes these arrivals for saviours.
arson-at-puharich-s-house-1978: A researcher named Greg, on Jesse Michels's podcast about a scientist with ties to the CIA, the US foreign intelligence agency, who is said to have contacted an alien council, says that this scientist, Puharich, had his house burn down in 1978 in Ossining, New York. Greg says the fire department proved it was arson, but to this day no one really knows who did it. He tells it as a hint that someone may have wanted to stop Puharich's work.
art-bell-s-material-said-to-come-from-ro: Roswell is a town in New Mexico where, people say, a strange craft came down in 1947. A podcast host, Jesse Michels, passes on a rumor that Art Bell, a late-night radio host, ended up with some material that Michels thinks came from that crash. He raises it with the scientist Garry Nolan, and if the rumor were true, physical pieces of the Roswell object would have reached private hands.
art-bell-s-satellite-transmission-failur: Art Bell, the host of a famous late-night American radio show called Coast to Coast AM, says that in 1997, during a call about Area 51, a secret US military base in Nevada, his whole satellite broadcast system suddenly failed. He says he was told the show was off the air. Listeners who tell the story see it as a sign that someone did not want that call heard.
arthur-c-clarke-s-sri-lanka-mountain-por: A podcast host, Jesse Michels, says that Arthur C. Clarke, the science fiction writer, wrote a book about a portal on top of a mountain in Sri Lanka. Michels brings it up while talking about strange experiences and other worlds, as if the writer had touched on something more than fiction.
arthur-c-clarke-says-nasa-found-large-li: A researcher guest on Jesse Michels's podcast says that around 2000 the science fiction writer Arthur C. Clarke, with the astronaut Buzz Aldrin present, said that NASA, the US space agency, had "basically discovered large forms of life on Mars." The guest passes this on as something Clarke said, because if true it would mean NASA was holding back proof of life on another planet.
arthur-young-puharich-and-the-seances-wi: A podcast host, Jesse Michels, says that an inventor named Arthur Young and a researcher named Andrija Puharich took part in séances, sessions meant to contact unseen beings, with a group that called itself the Nine. According to Michels, this went on in the United States sometime between the 1950s and the 1970s, and he tells it as a case of serious people trying to talk with a non-human intelligence.
arthur-young-s-quest-to-invent-the-bell-: A psychologist and interviewer named Jeffrey Mishlove, on Jesse Michels's podcast, tells the story of Arthur Young, the inventor behind the Bell helicopter. According to Mishlove, Young went to the patent office in Washington, the office that records inventions, to look for problems no one had solved, and picked the helicopter, working on it from the 1920s to the 1940s. Mishlove tells it to show the unusual mind of a man who later became interested in consciousness and the unexplained.
arthur-young-s-reflexive-universe-spirit: A researcher of the mind and the paranormal, Jeffrey Mishlove, describes the ideas of Arthur Young, an inventor and thinker who wrote a 1976 book called The Reflexive Universe. As Mishlove tells it, Young saw the whole universe as one process in which spirit comes down into physical matter and then matter rises back up into spirit. If right, it would mean that mind and spirit, not matter, sit at the root of everything.
arv-idea-comes-from-lazar-sorensen-and-m: Eric Davis, a physicist who has worked on government studies of unexplained craft, says on Jesse Michels's podcast that the idea of the ARV, short for alien reproduction vehicle, meaning a human-built craft said to copy alien technology, entered the thinking of UFO enthusiasts through a few men. He names Bob Lazar, Brad Sorensen and Mark McCandlish, each known for claims about secret craft. He means that the idea spread through their stories, which shapes how much weight it deserves.
arv-spelled-out-as-alien-reproduction-ve: Matthew Brown, who describes himself as a whistleblower from inside the Pentagon, says that a briefing he saw, around 2018, on the capabilities of a secret effort he calls Immaculate Constellation spelled out the letters ARV as "alien reproduction vehicle", to the best of his memory. Brown, who also mentions Lou Elizondo, a former Pentagon official who ran a UFO study effort, reads that wording as a possible counterintelligence marker, a detail placed to trace or steer how information spreads.
as-a-child-he-sensed-the-tube-tv-turning: Dan Sherman, a former US Air Force sergeant who says the National Security Agency, the US spy agency for communications, hired him to communicate with aliens, says that as a child he could always tell when the old tube television was switched on, even from another room of the family home. He tells it as an early sign of the unusual sensitivity he believes later made him useful for that work.
as-above-so-below-engraving-possibly-by-: A podcast host, Jesse Michels, describes an old engraving reading 'as above, so below', a saying from old mystical traditions, found at Skinwalker Ranch, a Utah property famous for reports of strange events. He says nobody knows who carved it, but suggests it may be the work of Augustus Walley, a famed Buffalo Soldier, as the Black US Army troops of the 1800s were called, who won the Medal of Honor. In a later episode he leaves out Walley's name and instead points out that the Buffalo Soldiers were Freemasons, a secret fraternal society, hinting that the carving holds hidden knowledge about the place.
ascent-through-the-seven-hekhalot-in-eno: Podcast host Jesse Michels points to the Book of Enoch, an ancient Jewish religious text, and the Merkavah texts, writings of ancient Jewish mystics. He says they describe a journey upward through seven 'hekhalot', meaning palaces, reached through breathing techniques, visualisation and chant-like prayers. He raises it as a sign that ancient people had practices for reaching other levels of reality.
asha-calls-spelling-pseudoscience: Ky Dickens, a filmmaker behind a documentary about nonspeaking children who are said to read minds, says the American Speech-Language-Hearing Association, a US professional body for speech therapists, rejects "spelling". That is a method where nonspeaking people point to letters to communicate. She says the association calls it not a valid form of communication and labels it pseudoscience, which matters because her children's stories come through that method.
asher-s-first-words-to-j-tune-into-my-he: A documentary filmmaker named Ky Dickens, who made a film about children who cannot speak but are said to read minds, told podcast host Jesse Michels about two people from her work, Asher and J. She says that the first thing Asher communicated to J was "tune into my heart." She tells it as part of the case that these children can connect with others without words.
asheville-viewer-s-videos-of-pulsating-l: Podcast host Jesse Michels reads out a message from a viewer in Asheville, North Carolina, in 2024. The viewer says they filmed pulsating lights in the sky the night before and have seven videos, about 30 minutes of good footage. Michels raises it as fresh evidence while challenging a UFO skeptic in a debate.
asis-operative-lent-to-mi6-to-bug-kuwait: An Australian journalist, Ross Coulthart, told podcast host Jesse Michels about a spying story from around 1991 that he reported in 1994. He says Britain's foreign spy service, MI6, secretly borrowed a technical bugging expert from Australia's foreign spy service, ASIS, to plant listening devices in Kuwaiti government offices. According to Coulthart, the British used this to win a business advantage over Australia itself, which shows how allied spy agencies can work against each other.
asked-to-blow-the-whistle-because-legacy: Matthew Brown, a former Pentagon official, tells podcast host Jesse Michels that around 2023 and 2024 people in his professional circle told him Congress needed whistleblowers. He says he came forward because a long-running secret programme, a so-called legacy program, was not being managed properly or overseen. If true, it would mean a hidden effort was running without proper checks from lawmakers.
asked-to-take-part-in-congressional-test: Dan Sherman, a former US Air Force sergeant who says the National Security Agency, the US spy agency for communications, hired him to communicate with aliens, says that in 2025 he was recently asked to take part in testimony before the US Congress. If it happens, his claims would be put on the official record in front of lawmakers.
asked-to-work-on-electron-flow-for-back-: Chris Bledsoe, a man who says UFOs appear around him and that NASA has studied him, says that a long time ago he was asked to work on which way electrons move. He links this to efforts at back-engineering, meaning taking apart unknown technology to learn how it works. To him, it shows that such work was underway long ago.
asking-mary-his-purpose-in-the-middle-ea: A man called Ralph, who says he served as a senior CIA officer, says that sometime between 2011 and 2016, while in the Middle East, he silently asked a presence he calls Mary why he was there. He says the answer came back without words: "You're here to be here." He tells it as a moment of guidance from beyond the ordinary, and mentions a Jesuit priest friend in connection with it.
assyrian-branch-settles-the-old-holy-lan: A researcher known as Matt, speaking on Jesse Michels's podcast in 2024, says he believes a branch of the Assyrians, an ancient people of the Middle East, moved into a part of eastern Turkey that he calls the "old Holy Land". He says this group was later destroyed. If true, the area would hold a forgotten chapter of sacred history.
asteroid-bennu-study-finds-nucleic-bases: On the podcast of host Jesse Michels, Eric Haseltine, introduced as a former director of the National Security Agency (the US spy agency that intercepts communications), mentions in passing a study of Bennu, an asteroid. As the story goes, that study found nucleic bases, the chemical letters that genetic material is built from. If true, it would suggest that the raw ingredients of life are scattered through space.
astra-on-the-skunk-works-org-chart-1993: A writer named Nick Cook, who has investigated claims of anti-gravity aircraft, says that in the mid-1990s he was shown an organisation chart for the Skunk Works, the secret aircraft design division of the company Lockheed in Palmdale, California. He says that above the familiar units on the chart he saw a name, Astra, and that he noted it in his diaries. If true, it would point to a hidden programme sitting over even the most secret aircraft work.
astral-experience-on-the-hill-after-zoom: A man named Jordan Jos, who says he was taken into a secret program as a child, describes a video call with someone who had appeared in The Telepathy Tapes, a documentary series about children said to read minds. Afterward, he says, he had an out-of-body experience in a place called "the hill," where he was shown an image of Ken, a non-verbal autistic boy who was in the same program with him at a place called Baker Victory. He tells it because it would link his childhood program to these mind-reading children.
astronaut-crew-quarters-something-came-b: A man named Chris Bledsoe, who says he attracts UFOs and has been studied by NASA, told podcast host Jesse Michels what a man named Timothy Taylor told him about the astronauts' living quarters at Cape Canaveral, the Florida rocket launch site. According to Bledsoe, Taylor said that every time a craft went up and came back down, something came back with the crew, and it was still there in those quarters. If true, it would mean early spaceflights brought some unseen presence back to Earth.
astronaut-says-the-moon-technology-was-d: An unnamed NASA astronaut is quoted saying he would gladly go to the moon again, but that the US no longer has the technology to do it. "We used to," he says, "but we destroyed that technology," a remark some take as a hint that something about the moon trips is being kept quiet.
astronaut-ufo-code-names-per-edgar-mitch: Podcast host Jesse Michels says a man in Japan named Takano Jouen, who was close to the Apollo astronaut Edgar Mitchell, told him something Mitchell had said. According to Jouen, Mitchell said astronauts in the 1960s and 70s used code names to talk about UFOs. If true, it would mean astronauts saw such things often enough to need a secret way to talk about them.
at-an-lax-pedestrian-death-all-sound-van: A writer named Brent Friedman tells a podcast host, Jesse Michels, about something he says happened in the 1980s at Los Angeles International Airport, known as LAX. He says he was there when a woman on foot was fatally hit. The airport is a very noisy place, he says, but in that moment he heard nothing except her breathing. He adds that time seemed to slow, and that at the moment she died, all the noise of the airport came rushing back. Brent is the only teller, describing it twice in the same interview. He tells it as a moment when ordinary reality seemed to fall away around a death.
at-t-breakup-testimony-before-judge-gree: Harold Malmgren, a former presidential advisor and trade official, tells podcast host Jesse Michels that in the early 1980s the phone company AT&T hired him as its final witness in the government case that broke the company up, heard in Washington by Judge Harold Greene. He tells it to show how close he stood to major decisions, which supports his claim to have handled UFO material directly.
at-the-table-with-john-mack-in-england-o: Joe McMoneagle, a guest on a podcast about alien life, says that in 2004 he sat at a table in England with a man named John Mack and talked with him. He says Mack died that same day. He tells it as a personal last meeting with a figure well known in these circles.
atf-attempt-to-link-guest-to-the-oklahom: A scientist named Steve, who studies objects some people believe are alien implants in human bodies, says that around 1995 the ATF, the US federal agency that deals with firearms and explosives, tried to tie him to the Oklahoma City bombing carried out by Timothy McVeigh. As near as he can figure, he says, the agency was punishing him for refusing to cooperate with one of its investigations. He tells it as an example of government pressure on him.
atlantean-survivors-may-live-among-us-wi: Podcast host Jesse Michels asks a researcher, Randall Carlson, whether survivors of Atlantis, the legendary lost civilisation, might still live among us, perhaps in bases under the sea or on the Moon. Carlson calls it a loaded question and answers that, very provisionally, yes. If true, it would mean an advanced lineage has stayed hidden from the rest of humanity since ancient times.
atlantic-article-on-obama-briefing-edite: Podcast host Jesse Michels says that in October 2010 the magazine The Atlantic wrote that President Obama had been briefed that morning on a power failure at F.E. Warren, an Air Force base in Wyoming. He quotes the article on an episode about UFOs seen near nuclear weapons bases, and suggests that its wording was later edited, which he finds telling.
atlantis-as-a-multi-site-ice-age-civiliz: Graham Hancock, a writer about lost ancient civilisations, says on Jesse Michels's podcast in 2024 that Atlantis, the lost civilisation from an ancient Greek tale, was probably more than one place. He suggests it was spread during the Ice Age across sites such as North America, the Azores islands, the Sahara, the Amazon and coastlines now under the sea, drawing on researchers Randall Carlson and Jimmy Corsetti. If so, an advanced worldwide culture existed long before recorded history.
atlantis-as-an-island-empire-on-the-mid-: A researcher of ancient catastrophes named Randall Carlson, on Jesse Michels's podcast, says that if the ancient Greek philosopher Plato's account of Atlantis, a legendary lost civilization, is even partly true, it describes an island empire in the middle of the Atlantic with advanced sailing and navigation skills. He places it on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, an underwater mountain chain, near the Azores islands, in the time of the ice age. Michels later repeated, citing Carlson, that he finds the Azores interesting, because it could mean an advanced lost civilization existed before recorded history.
atlantis-s-rebellion-and-the-flood: A philosopher named Jason Jorjani, speaking on a podcast hosted by Jesse Michels, says that the ancient Greek writer Plato, in his dialogues Timaeus and Critias, describes a rebellion in Atlantis, a lost civilization. According to Jorjani, Plato says the great sin of the Atlanteans was that they stopped worshipping the gods and making sacrifices to them, so Zeus called the Olympian gods together and decided to wipe the world clean in the flood better known as Noah's flood. If he is right, a famous myth and a Bible story would share one memory of a real lost civilization.
atlantis-search-atlantic-region-matching: Tim Gallaudet, a retired US Navy admiral, told the podcast host Jesse Michels that he and others have been searching for Atlantis, the lost island civilisation described by the ancient Greek philosopher Plato in his written dialogues. Gallaudet says they believe they have found a region in the Atlantic Ocean that fits all of Plato's descriptions, though he does not say where. If he is right, a legendary civilisation older than ancient Egypt would have a real location.
atlantis-search-presentation-to-victor-v: A former Navy admiral named Tim Gallaudet, speaking on Jesse Michels's podcast, says that sometime in the 2020s he and his colleagues gave a man named Victor Vescovo a presentation on searching the ocean for Atlantis, the legendary lost civilization. Gallaudet says Vescovo was interested and answered, "All right, I'm in," which would mean a real expedition to look for Atlantis had someone behind it.
atlas-launch-scrubbed-from-the-records-1: A man named Bob Jacobs says that in September 1964 an Atlas rocket was launched from Vandenberg Air Force Base in California, even though the official line was that there was no launch that day. According to Jacobs, a man named Robert later found Vandenberg's files describing that very launch in detail, which, if true, would mean the launch was quietly scrubbed from the record.
atomic-energy-act-s-special-nuclear-mate: A former US intelligence officer, David Grusch, says that the Atomic Energy Act of 1954, a US law that keeps nuclear matters secret, defines "special nuclear material" so broadly that it covers almost any material that gives off atomic energy, which he says would include material from crashed craft of unknown origin. A podcast host, Jesse Michels, repeats the point and goes further, saying the wording was chosen in a sneaky, deliberate way to protect UFO secrets, and that anything recovered is "born secret" under the law. If true, it would mean that an old nuclear law quietly keeps crash material hidden from the public.
atomic-energy-commission-born-secret-res: A podcast host, Jesse Michels, explains that the Atomic Energy Commission, the US agency set up after the Second World War to control nuclear matters, created a category called restricted data starting around 1946. According to him, anything collected that showed signs of radiation was 'born secret', meaning it was classified from the moment it existed. He brings it up because it would explain how material from unexplained objects could be hidden by law automatically.
atomic-energy-commission-contract-for-pu: On Jesse Michels' podcast, in an episode about a scientist said to have contacted an alien council, an unnamed guest says that in 1963 or 1964 this man, Puharich, got a contract from the Atomic Energy Commission, the US government agency then in charge of nuclear research. By this account, a man later tied to talk of alien contact was also doing work for official government science.
atomic-energy-commission-grant-to-intele: A researcher named Greg Malatzi, speaking on a podcast hosted by Jesse Michels, tells of a small company called Intelectron, based in the Hell's Kitchen neighbourhood of New York City in the early 1960s. He says it got a $300,000 grant, worth a million dollars or more today, from the Atomic Energy Commission, the US government agency that ran nuclear research at the time. He draws on the writer Annie Jacobsen and on the grant documents, and the point of the story is that, if true, the government took the company's unusual work seriously.
atomic-energy-commission-nuclear-secrecy: A podcast host, Jesse Michels, says that in the 1950s the Atomic Energy Commission, the US agency set up to run the country's nuclear work, was handling secrets at Los Alamos, the New Mexico lab where the atomic bomb was built, and at other nuclear sites. His sense is that UFO activity was going on around those same places, so the strict rules on nuclear secrets got laid on top of UFO secrets. If so, that would help explain why the UFO material stayed so tightly hidden.
attempted-abduction-and-face-cutting-of-: A man named Tim Alberino, who investigates strange creature reports, told podcast host Jesse Michels about events around 2023 in San Antonio de Pintuyacu, a village in the Peruvian Amazon. He says a 15-year-old girl named Talia was almost abducted and had her face cut, and that this is why the police went out to the village, a story he relays from a man named Doug. He tells it as evidence of real attacks by unknown beings on villagers there.
attempts-to-discredit-lazar-s-los-alamos: A podcast host, Joe Rogan, talking with another host, Jesse Michels, discusses Bob Lazar, a man who says he worked on alien craft in the 1980s at S4, a site said to be part of Area 51, the secret test base in Nevada. Rogan says critics tried to claim Lazar never worked at Los Alamos, the nuclear weapons laboratory in New Mexico, but that this has been confirmed, and that Lazar really was at S4. He draws on Lazar himself and on the journalist George Knapp, and if he is right, the attempts to discredit Lazar fall apart.
aubrey-marcus-had-a-dmt-experience-durin: A neuroscientist, Andrew Gallimore, tells podcast host Jesse Michels what a man named Aubrey Marcus told him about a darkness retreat, where a person spends days in total darkness. According to Gallimore, Marcus said that after the fourth or fifth day he had an experience that was not just like DMT, a powerful psychedelic substance, but was a full DMT experience. If true, it would suggest that darkness alone can open the same strange inner world the drug does.
audience-member-with-magnetic-ear-implan: A podcast host, Jesse Michels, says that at a live show he did with another podcast, Area 52, hosted by Chris Ramsey, an audience member told of a strange experience as a child. Michels says the man has something in his ear, similar to the implants discussed on the show, and a magnet held to the outside will stick to it. If true, it would be physical evidence tied to a childhood encounter.
aurora-black-triangle-program-1987: A podcast host, Jesse Michels, citing the writer Nick Cook, tells of Aurora, said to be a secret aircraft programme linked to sightings of black triangle-shaped craft over places like Groom Lake in Nevada and the North Sea from the late 1980s into the 1990s. Michels says Aurora showed up as a line item in the 1987 congressional budget with $2.3 billion set aside, which the aerospace company Lockheed had trouble explaining. He points to Jane's Defence Weekly, a defence trade magazine, and British Ministry of Defence papers, which would suggest the US was flying secret advanced craft if true.
aurora-budget-line-item-1980: On a podcast hosted by Jesse Michels, in an episode with a former US Secretary of Energy, it is said that a 1980s government budget had a line item called "Aurora." It is told as a hint of a secret program hidden inside the military's budget, which would mean advanced projects were funded out of public view.
aurora-in-the-1986-budget: Podcast host Jesse Michels talks about Aurora, said to be a secret American aircraft programme. He says it shows up as a line item in the 1986 US budget, for something like 2 billion dollars, and that British Ministry of Defence papers touch on it too. In the same conversation he mentions Ben Rich, a former head of Lockheed's secret aircraft division, and if the budget line is real it would mean a hidden advanced aircraft was being paid for.
aurora-rumoured-at-raf-machrihanish-1987: Nick Cook, a British aviation journalist, says on Jesse Michels's podcast that there were rumours about Aurora, a supposed secret American aircraft, in the late 1980s and 1990s. He says it was rumoured to be based for a while at RAF Machrihanish, a remote Royal Air Force base in Scotland. If true, a secret advanced aircraft would have been flying from British soil.
aurora-texas-airship-crash-and-alien-bur: A man named Chris Bledsoe, who says he attracts UFOs, told podcast host Jesse Michels about a story from Aurora, Texas, in 1897, which he calls the first such report he knows of in America. He says a flying ship crashed into a windmill tower there and the townspeople buried an alien from it. Bledsoe says the alien was buried right beside his own family's cemetery, which, if true, would tie his family to one of the oldest crash stories in the country.
austin-meeting-where-puthoff-said-skinwa: A writer named Peter Levenda, speaking on Jesse Michels's podcast, says he was at a meeting in Austin, Texas, with a group that included Tom DeLonge, Chris Mellon, Hal Puthoff, Jacques Vallee and John Alexander, where the talk turned to Skinwalker Ranch, a property in Utah known for reports of strange happenings. Levenda says Puthoff finally looked around and said they would need a SCIF, a specially secured room for classified discussions, for this one, which would suggest that what was known about the ranch was too sensitive to say out loud.
australian-aboriginal-oral-tradition-con: A scholar of religion, Diana Pasulka, says on Jesse Michels's podcast that indigenous friends told her about Australian Aboriginal culture. She says it holds a very old, compact oral tradition, perhaps around 30,000 years old, that deals with non-human intelligence, meaning beings that are intelligent but not human. If true, it would mean people have been telling stories of such contact for an extremely long time.
australian-man-leaves-edgar-mitchell-s-h: A documentary filmmaker, James Fox, says that after the death of Edgar Mitchell, an astronaut who walked on the moon, he caught an Australian man at Mitchell's house in Florida leaving with files. Fox links this to the Wilson memo, a document that comes up in talk of secret UFO programmes. If true, it would mean papers about such secrets were being quietly taken from a famous astronaut's home.
australian-man-records-astronaut-private: A man named Charlie Foltz, who tells of alien abduction experiences, told podcast host Jesse Michels about a man from Australia he once met. According to Foltz, this man had been recording radio traffic from early American astronauts, and when the astronauts switched to a different, private channel, he was able to switch too. The suggestion is that he caught things the astronauts said that were not meant for the public.
australian-officer-says-buchanan-also-kn: A former US Army sergeant, Lyn Buchanan, tells podcast host Jesse Michels about an earlier incident in which computers were said to have failed because of him. He says that years later, in a cafeteria at the Bureau of Indian Affairs, a US government agency, an Australian officer came up and told him: "you're the one that knocked out our computers over in Australia." If true, it would mean whatever power he had reached far beyond the first incident.
australian-special-forces-paid-cash-for-: An Australian investigative journalist, Ross Coulthart, tells podcast host Jesse Michels that members of Australian special forces told him they had been involved in operations to retrieve UAP, the official term for unidentified flying objects. According to the story, they were paid cash for helping the United States with these recoveries. If true, it would mean allied soldiers were quietly helping recover unknown craft.
autec-submersible-ufo-rumors-near-nassau: A podcast host, Jesse Michels, talks about AUTEC, a US Navy undersea testing and weapons training site in the Bahamas near Nassau, and says there are tons of rumors about it. In another episode he adds that there are underwater cables there that nobody can say where they lead. He raises it because the rumors suggest unknown craft or hidden activity moving under the sea.
autopsy-on-a-soldier-likely-wounded-by-a: In 1996, in the Brazilian town of Varginha, a story spread that a strange creature had been captured and that a young military policeman who helped catch it later died. A podcast host, Jesse Michels, says he interviewed the doctor who did the autopsy on that soldier, a man he calls Armando Fortunato. Michels names the soldier as Marco Chereze. He says Chereze seemed to die of a bacterial infection unlike anything seen before, and that he was likely hurt by a being from another world. The doctor himself tells it more carefully. He says that when the soldier's body came to the Forensic Medical Institute, nobody mentioned any contact with extraterrestrials. He says the autopsy was ordered to check whether another doctor had made a professional mistake. So the host and the doctor are the two voices here, one framing it as an alien story and the other recalling a routine inquiry, and if the host is right, a man died from touching a living alien.
avesta-s-island-continent-that-froze-ove: A researcher named Jason Jorjani told podcast host Jesse Michels about a passage in the Avesta, the ancient holy texts of Iran's old Zoroastrian religion. He says the Avesta tells that the Aryan people came from an island continent at the center of the world that froze over, which he links to Antarctica. If true, it would mean an ancient people remembered a homeland now buried under ice.
avi-loeb-s-calculation-against-fravor-s-: In a debate on Jesse Michels' podcast, a skeptic named Michael Shurmer brings up the account of David Fravor, a Navy fighter pilot. In 2004, off San Diego near the aircraft carrier USS Nimitz, Fravor says an unidentified object dropped from 80,000 feet to sea level almost instantly. Shurmer cites a calculation by a researcher, Avi Loeb, as an argument against that drop, which would point to technology far beyond anything known if it happened as described.
aviation-week-editor-threatened-over-sor: A UFO researcher who goes by the online name UAPGerb told podcast host Jesse Michels about an interview with a man named Sorensen published in the 1990s by Aviation Week, a magazine about aircraft and aerospace. UAPGerb says he later spoke with the editor of that interview, who told him the magazine received threats afterward, like the visits from mysterious "Men in Black" said to silence UFO witnesses. If true, it would suggest someone wanted that interview's subject kept quiet.
aviators-reports-to-graves-leading-to-th: Ryan Graves, a former US Navy fighter pilot who has spoken about seeing UFOs, says that after going public he became a beacon for people wanting to report their own sightings. He says most were pilots, though all sorts of people called. He describes this flood of reports as part of what led to a 2023 hearing in the US Congress on unexplained objects in the sky.
avro-car-in-nasa-wind-tunnel-1961: A podcast host, Jesse Michels, mentions the Avrocar, a round, saucer-shaped experimental aircraft, being tested in a NASA wind tunnel in 1961. He raises it in a talk about antigravity, as evidence that the US government was seriously working on flying-saucer designs.
avrocar-as-cover-for-roswell-craft-work-: A podcast host, Jesse Michels, suggests that the Avrocar, a saucer-shaped experimental aircraft built in Canada, was probably a cover for something deeper. He points to rumors that a craft said to have crashed near Roswell, New Mexico, in 1947 was taken to Wright Field, a US military airfield, and links the work to names such as John Frost, Richard Miethe, Viktor Schauberger and Henri Coanda. If true, it would mean the public saucer project hid secret study of a recovered craft and the recruitment of former Nazi scientists.
avrocar-project-moved-to-wright-pat-as-p: In the 1950s, according to a lawyer and researcher named Dan Sheehan, Canada ran a project called the Avrocar, which a podcast host, Jesse Michels, describes as an attempt to build a flying saucer. Sheehan says the project was then moved to Wright-Patterson, an Air Force base in Ohio, under the name Project Y bug. It is told to show that governments were trying to build saucer-shaped craft themselves.
axelrod-oni-nimitz-investigator-studying: A podcast host, Jesse Michels, says that a man who goes by the made-up name Axelrod was the chief investigator for the Office of Naval Intelligence, the US Navy's intelligence service, on the Nimitz case. That is a 2004 episode in which Navy crews from the aircraft carrier USS Nimitz reported an unexplained object. Michels says this same man now shows up at Skinwalker Ranch, a Utah property known for reports of strange happenings, to study them, which would mean someone from the Navy's own investigation has carried that work onto the ranch.
ayanis-andesite-foundation-under-mud-bri: A researcher known as Matt, on Jesse Michels's podcast in 2024, shows the foundation of Ayanis, an ancient fortress site in eastern Turkey, which has mud brick walls on top. He says the foundation is made of andesite, which he calls one of the hardest stones on Earth. His point is that the base may come from more skilled, older builders than the walls above it.
azores-as-sunken-mountain-tops-of-a-lost: A researcher, Randall Carlson, says the Azores, a group of islands in the middle of the Atlantic Ocean, are really the tops of sunken mountains. In his telling, during the late Ice Age, when sea levels were about 400 feet lower, those peaks belonged to a larger land that has since gone under, which would make the Azores the remains of a lost Mid-Atlantic land.
aztec-1948-craft-powered-up-at-wright-fi: This story is about a craft said to have crashed near Aztec, New Mexico, in March 1948 and to have been taken to Wright Field, a military airfield. A podcast host named Jesse Michels says that a firsthand witness claimed to have worked on that craft at Wright Field, and the story goes that when it was powered up it became see-through. Scott Ramsay, an author who wrote a book about the Aztec crash, says an engineer connected to the camera company Eastman Kodak contacted him and said he was pretty sure it was the craft he had worked on after reading Ramsay's book. People tell it because, if true, it would mean the military recovered a working craft that was not made by humans.
aztec-craft-taken-to-los-alamos-then-wri: A podcast host, Jesse Michels, drawing on a researcher named Scott Ramsay, tells of a craft said to have come down near Aztec, New Mexico, in 1948. According to Michels, it was first taken to Los Alamos, the government laboratory in New Mexico, and then moved to Wright Field, an Air Force base in Ohio. If true, it would mean the government quietly took a crashed craft and moved it between its own sites.
aztec-crash-and-its-debunking-1948: A UFO historian named Richard Dolan told podcast host Jesse Michels about a claimed crash of a flying saucer near Aztec, New Mexico, around 1948, which he calls the first such case ever written about, and says he believes it. He says the story was attacked and dismissed in the years after, that a writer named William Steinman wrote a big book on it, and that later researchers Scott and Suzanne Ramsey brought it back to respectability, even though the online encyclopedia Wikipedia still labels it fake. If true, it would be one of the earliest recovered crashed craft in America.
aztec-crash-possibly-brought-down-by-the: A researcher who goes by UAPGerb talks about a craft said to have crashed near Aztec, New Mexico, in 1948. He says one of the main theories is that it was brought down by the lashup radar network, an early chain of radar stations built over New Mexico to guard against Soviet bomber attacks. If true, it would mean military radar could knock such craft out of the sky.
b-2-bomber-money-diverted-to-illegal-man: Steven Greer, a campaigner who wants UFO secrets made public, says the B-2, an American stealth bomber, is billed at about $2 billion a plane when it probably costs less than $100 million to build. In his telling, the gap is money quietly moved into illegal secret projects that build man-made UFOs.
b-2-colonel-whispers-about-electrogravit: An author and UFO historian named Richard Dolan says that at a 2008 conference in Las Vegas, he was talking with a colonel connected to the B-2, an American stealth bomber, about electrogravitics, an idea that electric charge could be used to push against gravity. The talk touched on a paper by a researcher named Paul LaViolette linking the B-2 to that idea, and on the inventor Thomas Townsend Brown. Dolan says the colonel leaned forward and just whispered, "That's bullshit," a moment he tells because it hints at what insiders might privately think about the bomber's secrets.
b-2-uses-biefield-brown-effect-1992: The podcast host Jesse Michels says that in March 1992 Aviation Week, an aviation trade magazine, ran a story suggesting the B-2 stealth bomber uses the work of Townsend Brown, an inventor who studied how strong electric fields can create thrust, sometimes called electric gravity. In other episodes Michels leans on a biography, The Man Who Mastered Gravity by Paul Schatzkin, says Brown spread false versions of his own work to protect it, and says the plane's maker, Northrop Grumman, paid Brown a tiny sum for the rest of his life. If true, it would mean a form of anti-gravity research ended up in a real military plane.
baalbek-trilithon-stones: Jay Anderson, who talks about ancient sites, describes on Jesse Michels's podcast the trilithon at Baalbek in Lebanon, a set of three huge stones. He says they sit about 30 feet above the foundation blocks, are placed with precision, and weigh at least 800 tons each, possibly close to 1,000 tons. The size and precision raise the question of who could have moved them, and how.
baass-project-forum-and-ttsa-as-holdover: An online researcher who goes by UAPGerb tells podcast host Jesse Michels about documents from BAASS, a private aerospace contractor that ran a Pentagon-funded study of unexplained phenomena. He says the documents discuss something called Project Forum, a plan around 2011 in California to get celebrities, media personalities and other popular people talking about UFOs. He links this to To The Stars Academy, a later UFO company tied to the musician Tom DeLonge and former Pentagon official Luis Elizondo, as a kind of holdover, which if true would mean the public UFO conversation was partly steered on purpose.
baba-vanga-predicts-his-kalmykia-preside: A man who became president of Kalmykia, a republic within Russia, says that in the early 1990s he visited a Bulgarian fortune-teller known as Baba Vanga. He says she suddenly told him he would go back home and become its leader and president, and he mentions a telegram from Bulgaria tied to the visit, telling it as a prediction that came true.
baba-vanga-s-april-1995-prediction-of-th: A man who served as president of one of Russia's republics says that in April 1995 he got a call from Baba Vanga, a Bulgarian woman known as a seer, and her niece, telling him, "Kerson, come here." He tells it as the moment she foretold that he would become president of the world chess federation, and he also points to the Guinness book. If true, it would mean she could see what was coming before it happened.
baba-vanga-says-beings-live-underground-: A man described as the president of a Russian republic, who says he was taken by aliens in 1997, told podcast host Jesse Michels that he is certain beings live underground. He says a Bulgarian woman known as Baba Vanga told him so in the 1990s, sometimes pointing down with her finger and saying "they are talking there, they are there." If true, it would mean other beings share the Earth with us beneath our feet.
baba-vanga-talks-with-souls-and-entities: A man introduced as the president of a Russian republic says that in the 1990s he visited Baba Vanga, a woman in Bulgaria said to speak with souls and unseen beings, in her yard. He says he asked her whether we are alone, and she gave him a little smack and asked if he was stupid, because the beings were all around him, absolutely everywhere. If true, it would mean other beings share our world with us, and we simply fail to notice them.
babson-louis-witten-and-bryce-dewitt-gra: Eric Weinstein, a researcher speaking on Jesse Michels's podcast in 2024, says that in the 1950s a man named Babson contacted Louis Witten, a physicist then coming out of Johns Hopkins University. According to Weinstein, this led to gravity research institutes involving Witten and another physicist, Bryce DeWitt, including at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. He tells it as a sign of quiet early interest in mastering gravity.
babson-s-gravity-research-foundation-in-: In the 1950s, a man named Roger Babson ran something called the Gravity Research Foundation in New Boston, New Hampshire. A researcher, Eric Weinstein, says the official reason given for it, that Babson's sister had drowned in a pond, does not seem very believable to him. A podcast host, Jesse Michels, calls Babson a patron of science who was obsessed with solving anti-gravity, meaning ways to cancel gravity. They tell it as a sign that serious private money was chasing anti-gravity, perhaps for reasons not openly stated.
backlash-over-the-2021-transients-paper-: An astronomer named Beatriz Villarroel, who looks for unexplained objects in the sky, says that in 2021 her team found nine transients, points of light that show up in old sky images and then vanish. She says she published the paper with a colleague, Jeff Marcy, an astronomer who had been pushed out of the field over a sexual harassment scandal in 2015. According to her, working with him brought a backlash in the astronomy world that coloured how people received the discovery.
bae-colleagues-on-the-program-assume-bor: A man named Dylan Borland, who says he worked at BAE Systems, a large defense and aerospace company, says that in the 2010s some colleagues heard him talking about a triangle-shaped craft. He says they were part of a secret program themselves and assumed he had been "read in", meaning officially cleared and briefed on it. According to Borland, that assumption is how his whole involvement began.
bae-falcon-works-joint-ventures-with-loc: Dylan Borland, a man who says he worked at the defense company BAE Systems, says BAE has a unit called Falcon Works, its own version of Skunk Works, the secretive advanced aircraft division of the defense company Lockheed Martin. He says the two run joint projects on materials, engineering, engines and more, which, if true, would mean the two firms share their most advanced work.
baghdad-phantom-mission-report-released-: A journalist and filmmaker named Jeremy Corbell, speaking on a podcast hosted by Jesse Michels, talks about a military mission report on a case known as the Baghdad Phantom, set in Baghdad, Iraq. Corbell says the report was not supposed to be declassified, meaning made public, until 2047, but that it has come out early. If that is so, it would mean records about this case are reaching the public decades ahead of schedule.
baghdad-phantom-seven-still-images-then-: A filmmaker, Jeremy Corbell, told podcast host Jesse Michels about an unexplained object over Baghdad, Iraq, that he calls the Baghdad Phantom. He says that he and TV journalist George Knapp first released seven still images of it, and that around three years later video of it appeared in the government's first official release of such footage. If true, it would mean the government confirmed something the two had already reported.
bahamas-yacht-trips-with-eldridge-reeves: A podcast host, Jesse Michels, drawing on the book A Man Called Intrepid, tells of a circle that included a researcher named Townsend Brown and a man named William Stephenson. He says they went on trips to the Bahamas on a yacht owned by a man named Eldridge Reeves Johnson. He brings it up to suggest these figures were tied together in a hidden network behind the UFO story.
bahnsen-s-notes-on-unexplained-effect-19: A writer named Paul Schatzkin, who studies the inventor Townsend Brown, told podcast host Jesse Michels about notes kept in the 1950s in Chapel Hill, North Carolina, by a man named Agnew Bahnsen, who worked with Brown's devices. Schatzkin says Bahnsen wrote in his notes that something was going on in the experiments that they could not account for. If true, it would suggest Brown's work produced an effect that ordinary science could not explain.
