McKinnon says he took it to mean people based off Earth, like a secret space force, rather than aliens, which would point to a hidden fleet and supply chain in space.
the-nrol-16-patch-and-ron-pandolfi-2005: Podcast host Jesse Michels relays a case described by John Ramirez, a former officer of the CIA, the US spy agency, in a presentation. It concerns NROL-16, a 2005 launch for the National Reconnaissance Office, the US agency that runs spy satellites, and its mission patch, the cloth emblem made for the launch, which Ramirez links to a man named Ron Pandolfi. Michels tells it as an example of hidden symbolism tied to the UFO subject carrying on into the 21st century.
the-occult-is-behind-the-cover-up-of-gia: Tim Alberino, a filmmaker and researcher speaking on podcast host Jesse Michels's show, believes that giants, very large human-like beings, have existed and that their existence is being hidden. He says he thinks the occult, meaning secret mystical groups and practices, is behind that cover-up.
the-open-doors-von-neumann-s-fear-at-his: Whitley Strieber, an author known for writing about his own encounters with strange beings, says on a podcast that he wrote a short story called "The Open Doors" about the death of John von Neumann, a leading mathematician and scientist, in 1957. Strieber ties the story to a fear von Neumann is said to have held at the end of his life, which he links to the idea that some lines of physics research were deliberately sent down a dead end.
the-osirion-at-abydos-predates-seti-i: At Abydos in Egypt there is an ancient stone structure called the Osirion, which sits beside the temple of the pharaoh Seti I. Luke Caverns, a researcher speaking on podcast host Jesse Michels's show, says he does not believe Seti I built it and thinks it is far older. If so, it would mean someone built it long before the Egyptians usually credited with it.
the-osiris-shaft-scan-picks-up-something: A researcher named Jeffrey Drum, speaking on the podcast of host Jesse Michels in 2026, describes scans made in the 2020s of the Osiris Shaft, a deep shaft on the Giza Plateau in Egypt near the pyramids. He says the scan is "picking up something else" on the left side of the shaft, which would mean there is more hidden underground at Giza than is known.
the-pineapple-target-during-a-remote-vie: A podcast host, Jesse Michels, says that around 2023 or 2024 he sat in on a remote viewing session with Joe McMoneagle, a well-known practitioner. Remote viewing is the claimed ability to describe a hidden or distant target using only the mind. Michels says a friend of his drew a little spiky thing, and the hidden target turned out to be a pineapple, which he offers as something he experienced himself.
the-plants-told-the-amazonians-how-to-ma: A neuroscientist, Andrew Gallimore, says that when people in the Amazon are asked how they learned to make ayahuasca, a vision-inducing brew made from local plants, they answer that the plants told them. He raises it because, taken at face value, it would mean knowledge can come from something beyond ordinary human discovery.
the-prince-of-liechtenstein-walked-up-to: Dan Sheehan, a lawyer, says on a podcast that Laurance Rockefeller, a wealthy philanthropist, once told him and others, including the psychiatrist John Mack, why he was so convinced UFOs were real. According to Sheehan, Rockefeller said his friend, the Prince of Liechtenstein, had seen one, walking up to it somewhere in the mountains. For Sheehan, it shows that a powerful man's belief rested on a trusted friend's own encounter.
the-ra-channelings-and-the-law-of-one-19: Jeffrey Mishlove, a researcher and interviewer who studies psychic phenomena, told podcast host Jesse Michels about the Ra material, messages said to come from a being called Ra through channeling, where a person speaks on behalf of a non-human source, in the 1980s. He says Carla Rueckert, who took part along with a person named Bharich, published them as The Ra Material and The Law of One. Followers treat them as a teaching from non-human intelligence about the nature of reality.
the-range-dod-testing-playground-in-the-: Jake Barber, a former military helicopter pilot who says he once helped retrieve a UFO, tells podcast host Jesse Michels about where he worked after 2001. He describes "the range" in the California desert as a giant playground where the US Department of Defense and its private aerospace partners tested weapons technology. It is the setting he gives for the secret work he describes.
the-remote-viewing-photo-protocol-and-it: A podcast host, Jesse Michels, talks about remote viewing, the claimed ability to describe a distant place or a hidden photo using only the mind, which was tested with photos from the 1970s to the 1990s at the Stanford Research Institute, a research lab in California. He says a review of these attempts, citing a researcher named Jessica Utts, found an overall hit rate of 35 percent, a number repeated again and again, including at the University of Edinburgh and at the Rhine Research Institute at Duke in North Carolina. If true, it would suggest the mind can pick up information beyond the ordinary senses.
the-retrieved-craft-may-have-been-a-livi: John Blitch, a scientist who says he once worked with DARPA, the US military's research agency, spoke with podcast host Jesse Michels in 2025. Drawing on what a man named Jake Barber has said about a recovered unknown craft, Blitch suggests the craft itself "could have been a living being". If true, it would mean such craft are not just machines but alive in some way.
the-rosicrucian-enlightenment-and-the-in: A podcast host, Jesse Michels, recommends a book by Frances Yates called The Rosicrucian Enlightenment. The book is about the Rosicrucians, a secretive mystical movement in 17th-century Europe, and about the Invisible College, an informal circle of English thinkers that he links to the scientist Robert Boyle. He brings it up to suggest that hidden circles of thinkers may have helped shape modern science.
the-sapphire-project-and-hal-puthoff: On a 2025 episode of host Jesse Michels's podcast, a guest named Jay Anderson mentions something he calls the Sapphire project, linked to a researcher named Hal Puthoff. As Anderson tells it, efforts like this appeared briefly, with people feeling they were about to reach the stars, and then were "gone", which would suggest promising work that quietly disappeared.
the-sar-team-s-first-international-confe: Jeffrey Drum, a researcher, explains how he got involved with a team using SAR, a kind of radar imaging done from satellites, that claims to have found structures beneath the pyramids of Egypt. He says the team, which includes people named Armando and Filippo Biondi, held its first international conference in Malta in June 2025, and that its organizers already knew his work. It is his account of how he came to join their findings.
the-septuagint-reads-angels-of-god-in-ge: Tim Alberino, a filmmaker and researcher, points to the Septuagint, an ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible. He says that in Genesis 6, a passage in the Bible's first book, the Septuagint does not say "the sons of God" but "the angels of God." He raises it because it would mean the beings in that passage were understood as angels rather than men.
the-serapeum-as-a-sonohydrogen-plant: Geoffrey Drumm, a guest on host Jesse Michels's podcast, offers his idea about the Serapeum, an underground complex of huge stone boxes at Saqqara in Egypt. He says his hypothesis is that it used ultrasound, very high-pitched sound, to break water into hydrogen and oxygen, which would make it an ancient energy plant rather than a burial site.
the-shroud-image-was-made-by-a-burst-of-: Whitley Strieber, an author known for writing about strange encounters, calls the Shroud of Turin, an old linen cloth bearing the faint image of a man and believed by many to be Jesus's burial cloth, the single strangest thing on Earth. He says it records the moment a dead human body transformed into a being of light, with the image made by a burst of neutrons at the resurrection in Jerusalem. If true, it would mean the cloth is a physical record of a person's body changing into something else.
the-sphinx-as-a-dynastic-monument-carved: A researcher named Jeffrey Drum, talking with podcast host Jesse Michels in 2026, gives his view of the Great Sphinx at Giza in Egypt. He says he thinks the Sphinx is a monument from the time of the pharaohs, but that it was built on a bedrock outcrop that already existed in the Sphinx's enclosure, which would mean the site itself is older than the statue.
the-ss-never-surrendered-1945: The SS was the Nazi party's own armed and security force in Germany during the Second World War. A researcher named Jason Jorjani tells podcast host Jesse Michels that the German documents of surrender signed in 1945 do not include the SS. He raises it in a talk about a secret Nazi flying-saucer program, as a hint that part of the SS may have carried on after the war.
the-sun-as-a-scalar-wave-generator-sendi: A podcast host, Jesse Michels, floats the idea that the Sun might be a generator of scalar waves, a proposed kind of energy wave outside ordinary physics. He suggests that, if so, we might be receiving information from the Sun. That would make the Sun a source of messages rather than just light and heat.
the-teacher-born-in-george-washington-s-: Charles Hall, who says he spent three years in the 1960s among tall white beings at a remote US Air Force range in Nevada, describes a being he calls the Teacher. He says that in 1965, at Range Two in Indian Springs Valley, the Teacher, who he says was born around the time George Washington was born, remembered a Native American friend. If true, it would mean these beings live for centuries.
the-telepathy-tapes-nonverbal-autistic-i: The Telepathy Tapes is a 2024 podcast series about autistic people who cannot speak. An analyst named Matthew Pines describes it on Jesse Michels's podcast as the story of dozens of such people who are said to share a telepathic link with one caregiver, usually their mother. He credits the work of a doctor named Diane Hennacy Powell. If true, it would mean minds can pass thoughts directly to each other. A scientist, Don Hoffman, says he has seen studies in which an autistic child who can barely control their body reads what is in their mother's mind, and that some of the experiment designs looked fairly rigorous to him. A retired Navy admiral, Tim Gallaudet, also points to Powell's work with autistic patients, framing it as her own research over many years rather than as the podcast. So three separate guests bring it up, each on their own terms.
the-thera-santorini-theory-of-atlantis: A researcher, Randall Carlson, describes the idea that the huge volcanic eruption on the Greek island of Thera, now called Santorini, was the real event behind Atlantis, the lost land described by the Greek philosopher Plato. He points out that the eruption happened about 900 years before Plato. He raises it to weigh what the Atlantis story might really remember.
the-three-body-problem-as-required-readi: Podcast host Jesse Michels says Pippa Malmgren, an economist and daughter of presidential adviser Harald Malmgren, told him that high-level talks in Washington about disclosure, meaning the government revealing what it knows about non-human intelligence, kept circling back to one book. That book is The Three-Body Problem, a Chinese science fiction novel about first contact with aliens, which she says became mandatory reading for many top US national security advisers in the 2000s and 2010s. If true, it suggests officials were using fiction to think through real contact.
the-three-girls-who-saw-the-creature-wer: In 1996, in the Brazilian town of Varginha, three girls say they saw a strange creature that many took to be an alien. A surgeon named Italo Venturelli tells podcast host Jesse Michels that nurses who know the girls say they have had a hard time since. According to him, people criticized them and they were bullied so badly they had to change schools.
the-tic-tac-as-an-unrepeatable-anomaly-t: The Tic Tac is a white oval object, shaped like the mint, that US Navy pilots say they saw in the sky. A young researcher named Deep Prasad tells podcast host Jesse Michels that it poses a problem for the scientific method laid out by the old English thinker Francis Bacon, which relies on repeating experiments. He says the Tic Tac showed up once and cannot be made to happen again, yet it clearly needs to be studied, an idea he links to a written work called The Evolution of Science and the Interactive Universe.
the-top-hat-craft-with-projectile-holes-: Bob Lazar, a man who says he worked on alien craft in 1988 and 1989 at S-4, a secret site in Nevada, tells podcast host Jesse Michels about two of the craft he says he saw there, one he calls the top hat and one shaped like a Jell-O mold. He says the top hat had a hole in its rim, with the metal clearly bent outward as if it had been shot from below. He adds that a film about him got it wrong by showing two holes instead of one, and says that if true, someone had shot at one of these craft.
the-trinity-test-as-the-hinge-point-that: A podcast host, Jesse Michels, points to July 16, 1945, when the physicist Robert Oppenheimer's team set off Trinity, the first atomic bomb test, in the New Mexico desert. Michels frames that test as the turning point that drew the UFO phenomenon to us. If true, it would mean the visitors showed up because humanity had just gained the power to destroy itself.
the-underworld-in-the-kalmyk-epic-jangar: The president of a Russian republic, interviewed by a podcast host, Jesse Michels, points to Jangar, the old epic poem of the Kalmyk people of Kalmykia in southern Russia. He says the epic describes an underworld: the creatures that live there, how they communicate and how they come up to the surface. If he is right, it would suggest that ancient tradition remembers beings living beneath the earth.
the-vatican-archives-head-knows-about-th: Danny Sheehan, a lawyer, tells podcast host Jesse Michels that the head of the Vatican archives, the Catholic Church's records in Rome, knows about hidden material kept there. He says he knows this because he sent the letters himself, from the headquarters of the Jesuits, a Catholic religious order, asking for access for President Jimmy Carter. If true, it would mean a US president tried to see secret material held by the Church.
the-vatican-s-sun-cross-and-pine-cone: A researcher called Matt, speaking on host Jesse Michels's podcast in 2024, points to symbols at the Vatican, the home of the Catholic Church. He says the Pope wears the very same sun cross on his cloak that appears in older traditions, and that a giant pine cone stands in front of the Vatican, suggesting the Church carries on much older symbols.
the-wow-signal-1977: A podcast host, Jesse Michels, recalls the famous Wow signal, a radio signal that he says a radio telescope at Ohio State University picked up in August 1977, and that he credits to an astronomer named Gerry Ehman. It is told as a possible message from beyond Earth. If true, it would mean someone out there was sending signals.
theoretical-physicists-at-s4-had-exhaust: Bob Lazar, a man who says he worked on alien craft at S-4, a secret Nevada site, in 1988 and 1989, talks with podcast host Jesse Michels about the scientists there. He says the theoretical physicists had kept trying the same gravity-based ideas to explain how the craft worked and never got anywhere. The talk brings in the researchers Eric Weinstein and Eric Davis, and the point is that, as he tells it, the craft defeated the experts trying to understand them.
theory-non-humans-seed-and-genetically-a: Chris Ramsay, a guest on host Jesse Michels's podcast in 2025, lays out a theory that non-human beings seed life on planets and adjust it genetically. He suggests they then return every thousand years or so to introduce things like agriculture, irrigation, metal-working or religion, which would mean human progress has been guided from outside.
theory-that-directed-energy-forces-trans: A man named Jordan, who says he was taken into a secret UFO program as a child, offers a theory about objects that move between dimensions. He says that hitting such an object with directed energy, meaning focused beams of energy used as a weapon, forces it to take solid form and become bound to our dimension. If true, it would explain how such objects could be caught or brought down.
theory-that-nuclear-fuels-were-used-to-a: A podcast host, Jesse Michels, puts forward the idea that in the 1950s nuclear fuels were used at US nuclear bases to alter gravity. He notes that in general relativity, Einstein's theory of gravity, gravity and time are linked, so time might have been changed too, and he connects the idea to Dark, a time-travel series on Netflix. If true, it would explain why strange things gather around nuclear sites.
theory-that-oppenheimer-s-security-heari: A podcast host, Jesse Michels, floats the idea that the security hearing held for Robert Oppenheimer, the physicist who led the atomic bomb work, was secretly about UFOs. He calls it a kangaroo court and notes that it was headed by a man named Gordon Gray, a name that, he says, also appears in the Majestic 12 document, a paper said to describe a secret group overseeing UFO matters, alongside figures like the mathematician John von Neumann. If true, it would mean one of the best-known security cases in American history hid a UFO secret.
theory-that-shooter-valente-was-awaiting: A podcast host, Jesse Michels, discusses a shooter named Valente, in a December 2025 story that touches Boston, Providence and Brooklyn. Michels suggests that Valente may have been waiting for instructions, given to him either openly or subliminally. If true, it would mean someone else was directing him.
theory-that-the-object-was-built-before-: Dennis Asberg, a treasure hunter whose team found a strange shape on the floor of the Baltic Sea between Sweden and Finland, talks about where it might have come from. He suggests it was made a long time ago, perhaps before the last ice age. If true, it would mean someone built it far earlier than any known civilization.
theresa-may-withdraws-extradition-order-: In 2012, Theresa May, then the British government minister in charge of policing and borders, told the UK Parliament that she had withdrawn the extradition order against a man named McKinnon, meaning he would not be sent to another country to face trial. On Jesse Michels's podcast McKinnon is presented as a hacker who says he found signs of a secret NASA space program, so the decision is told as the end of his fight to avoid prosecution.
think-tank-conference-on-crash-retrieval: Jesse Michels, a podcast host, relays something told to him by Hal Puthoff, a physicist long involved in government research on unusual phenomena. According to Michels, a think-tank meeting in Washington DC worked from the premise that Russia, China and the United States had each recovered crashed craft of non-human origin. If true, it would mean several rival powers are quietly holding such material.
third-download-two-hours-of-experiencing: A man named Brent describes what he calls his third download, a sudden flood of information that he says came to him after a formula he had been given resurfaced. He says that for two hours his whole world shattered and he was experiencing multiple timelines at once. He tells it as something that happened to him personally, though he gives no time or place.
third-mission-where-shots-were-fired: Jake Barber, a former military helicopter pilot who says he took part in secret missions to retrieve UFOs, tells podcast host Jesse Michels about a later mission. He says that on that next mission shots were fired, and in a second interview he calls it an ambush. If true, it would mean these recovery missions were met with armed resistance.
third-strand-dna-manuscript-blocked-2022: A man named Dave Rossi, a guest on podcast host Jesse Michels's show in an episode about aliens teaching him advanced physics, says that two or three years earlier, around 2022, he wrote a manuscript about a "third strand" of DNA, meaning a strand beyond the usual two. He says someone was willing to help him get it into peer-reviewed form, the format where other scientists check work before it is published, but that this person was then "restrained" from helping. If true, it would suggest someone was quietly blocking his ideas from reaching scientists abroad.
thomas-bearden-and-soviet-scalar-death-r: A podcast host named Jesse Michels talks about Thomas Bearden, a man he describes as a Navy man who often spoke about "scalar weapons", a kind of weapon based on an unusual idea of energy fields. Michels says Bearden claimed the Soviet Union, during the Cold War, had worked out something like a huge death ray. If true, it would mean a rival superpower had built a weapon far beyond known physics.
thomas-townsend-brown-s-thrust-from-asym: A podcast host, Jesse Michels, tells of Thomas Townsend Brown, an American inventor of the mid-1900s. Michels says Brown found that putting a high voltage across certain lopsided capacitors, which are electrical parts that store charge, made them push themselves forward. If true, it would point to a way of moving a craft without rockets or propellers.
thomas-winterton-s-scalp-separated-from-: Thomas Winterton, introduced as the owner of Skinwalker Ranch, a property in Utah known for reports of strange happenings, told podcast host Jesse Michels about something that happened to him after he dug on the land. He says that three days after a day of digging he found a big lump, a "goose egg", on the back of his head, and the story as told is that his scalp had come away from his skull. He tells it as a sign that disturbing the ground there can hurt the people who do it.
thousands-of-ayahuasca-users-report-meet: Ayahuasca is a plant brew from the Amazon that people drink for strong visions. A researcher named Luke Caverns tells podcast host Jesse Michels that there are thousands of reports of people on ayahuasca meeting the same goddess, a woman who knows at once everything that is wrong with you. If true, it would hint that the visions show something real that many people meet, not just private dreams.
threats-against-asberg-and-his-family-ov: Dennis Asberg, a Swedish treasure hunter, says his team found an odd object on the floor of the Baltic Sea in 2011, which people now call the Baltic Sea anomaly. He told podcast host Jesse Michels that since then he has received emails threatening him and his children. He tells it to show how heated things got around the find.
threats-on-mount-rushmore-in-the-securit: Mario Woods, an Air Force veteran who guarded nuclear weapons, recalls a security briefing from 1977 at Ellsworth Air Force Base in South Dakota, near the Mount Rushmore monument. He says the briefing warned of threats against Mount Rushmore and of people who wanted to blow up a site. He gives it as background to the tense time when, he says, he and other airmen were taken by aliens.
three-9-foot-skeletons-vanish-overnight-: A man named Tim Alberino tells podcast host Jesse Michels about something that, he was told, happened around 1978 to 1981 at the Church of Santa Anastasia on the Italian island of Sardinia. According to his account, a man laid out three skeletons there, each at least 9 feet tall, and the next day they were gone. It is told as evidence that giants once lived, and that the proof keeps vanishing.
three-body-problem-as-chinese-soft-discl: David Grusch, a former US intelligence officer who has said the government holds non-human craft, told podcast host Jesse Michels he finds it "pretty trippy" that China allowed The Three-Body Problem, a science fiction series by a Chinese author about contact with aliens, to be published. He hints it could be a form of soft disclosure, a government quietly preparing the public through fiction. If so, China would be signalling what it knows.
three-brazilian-ufo-episodes-overseen-by: Aldo Rebelo, introduced on Jesse Michels's podcast as a former Brazilian Defense Minister, says Brazil has had hundreds of UFO episodes, and that at least three were closely watched by the armed forces and the country's intelligence and defense services. The cases are linked to the state of Pará, the city of São José dos Campos, and the town of Varginha, between the 1970s and 1990s. If true, it means Brazil's military took these events seriously enough to follow them itself.
three-bright-transients-on-19-july-1952-: An astronomer named Beatriz Villarroel studies old glass photographic plates from the Palomar Observatory in California, which recorded the night sky in the 1950s, and she looks for points of light that show up once and then vanish. On a podcast with host Jesse Michels, she says her colleague in Spain, Enrique Solano, found what she calls the most beautiful example of all: three very bright star-like points on a plate from 19 July 1952. If such flashes were real objects, they would point to something unexplained in the sky near Earth before any satellites had been launched.
three-campers-frozen-and-abducted-at-a-l: A former Army sergeant named Lyn Buchanan, speaking on a podcast hosted by Jesse Michels, says he once saw the record of an event in classified study materials. According to that record, three men were camping at a lake one night when they were frozen in place and taken away by something not human. Buchanan doesn't say when or where this happened, but he tells it as a case that ended up in official files, which would mean someone in government was keeping track of abductions.
three-dreams-within-a-dream-numbers-seve: A man called Ralph, presented on podcast host Jesse Michels's show as a former CIA chief, says that in 1991 at Mount Athos, a monastery peninsula in Greece, he had three dreams nested inside a dream: one about numbers, one about seven doors, and one about walking on water. In the last, he says, he was halfway across the water when an old woman beside him stumbled, he grabbed her arm, both were swept away, and he woke up. He links this to his claim that he travelled back in time to 14th-century Mount Athos.
three-fingered-mummies-in-peru: A podcast host, Joe Rogan, says that "now we have three-fingered mummies in Peru." Another podcast host, Jesse Michels, says he has seen these beings in Peru himself, skeletons with three fingers, and dates them to somewhere between 800 and 1,700 years ago. If they are what these men suggest, they would be the remains of beings that weren't human.
three-flying-saucers-over-a-church-at-de: Mario Woods, an Air Force veteran who later guarded nuclear weapons, says that in 1961, when he was about six, his mother pointed at the sky near De Queen Elementary School in Port Arthur, Texas, and said, "Look at those flying saucers." He says there were three of them, beautiful, hovering just 25 to 50 feet over a church. In a later telling he names his mother and his sister as fellow witnesses, and he tells it as the start of a lifetime of strange encounters.
three-foot-object-with-buttons-lying-on-: Joe McMoneagle, a man who says he did psychic "remote viewing" work for the US military, describes an object on Mars about three feet long with buttons on it. He links it to photo negatives from the Mars mapping done by JPL, the NASA laboratory that runs many space missions. If true, it would suggest something built by intelligent beings once sat on Mars.
three-girls-encounter-creature-near-mara: In Varginha, a town in Brazil, on 20 January 1996, a strange creature was reportedly seen, and this story is one part of that case. James Fox, a UFO investigator, says that near a military roadblock, three young girls named Valquiria, Liliane and Katia had "an encounter of the third kind," meaning they came face to face with a being. A podcast host, Jesse Michels, adds that the girls are grown women now and all still say they saw it. If true, a living non-human creature was walking around a Brazilian town.
three-gravity-emitters-on-the-sports-mod: A podcast host, Jesse Michels, retells a claim by Bob Lazar, a man who says he worked on alien craft in 1988 and 1989 at S4, a secret site in the Nevada desert. Michels says Lazar described three cylinder-shaped "emitters" at the base of one craft, nicknamed the sports model, and that he did so years before the gravity research of a scientist named Ning Li became public. Michels tells it because, if true, Lazar's account would seem to have predicted later science.
three-illuminated-plus-signs-over-stockh: Clas Svahn, a Swedish researcher who has collected UFO reports for decades, says that in November 1995 he and his wife Annalie saw three lit-up shapes like plus signs in the sky over a suburb of Stockholm. He tells it as his own sighting, which matters because he usually studies other people's.
three-light-beings-at-the-foot-of-his-ic: Brent Friedman is a Hollywood writer. On the podcast of host Jesse Michels, he says that about five years ago, during COVID, he was in a hospital intensive care unit with sepsis, a life-threatening reaction of the body to infection. One night, lying there alone, he says light beings suddenly came to the foot of his bed, three of them. If true, it would mean beings of light visit people near death. He mentions it again on a later episode of the same show, describing being on his deathbed and watching light beings come to the foot of his bed. That second telling gives no number of beings and no date, and its notes tie it to a cancer illness rather than COVID. Both tellings are Brent's own, given on two different episodes.
three-separate-intelligence-sources-told: A researcher named Bryce, speaking on Jesse Michels's podcast about Hollywood and UFOs, relays a story about Ross Coulthart, a journalist who reports on UFO secrecy. According to Bryce, three separate intelligence sources told Coulthart within a short time that if he really wanted to understand what was going on, he should watch Dark, a Netflix science fiction series. The point of telling it is the hint that insiders might be steering people toward the ideas in that show.
three-unidentified-objects-shot-down-in-: A researcher, Pippa Malmgren, recalls the week in 2023 when a Chinese balloon was in the news over North America. She says that in that same week the military said it shot down three other unidentified objects. She brings it up because, if those objects were never explained, it would mean unknown things were flying in guarded airspace.
three-way-telepathy-experiment-between-l: Blake Lemoine, an engineer who worked at Google, tells podcast host Jesse Michels about an experiment he says he ran around 2021 or 2022. He says he tested Google's artificial intelligence chat system, called LaMDA, together with a person who claims to have telepathic abilities, reading minds without speech. He tells it as part of his view that the system might be a kind of alien mind.
three-witnesses-held-at-gunpoint-and-giv: An online UFO researcher who goes by UAPGerb, speaking with podcast host Jesse Michels, tells of three men in the US military who saw something strange, were held at gunpoint, and then, he says, were all given shots they were told were anthrax vaccine boosters, a vaccine against a dangerous disease. He links the account to a man named Jonathan Wagant and gives no time or place. If true, it would suggest the military treated these encounters as something to contain and perhaps to hide medically.
three-women-see-the-red-eyed-being-1996: A podcast host, Jesse Michels, tells of 1996 in the town of Varginha, Brazil, where three women say they saw a strange being. According to Michels, who says the women seemed very honest to him, the creature had red eyes and brown skin. If true, it would be a close sighting of a living being that is not human.
thule-society-founder-initiated-in-kurdi: A researcher named Jason Jorjani, speaking with podcast host Jesse Michels in 2025, talks about the Thule Society, a secret society in early 20th century Germany. He says it was founded by a man named Baron Rudolf von Sebottendorf, who had been initiated into secret teachings in Kurdistan "of all places", hinting at a hidden link between that region and the German group.
thule-society-seances-to-contact-star-be: A podcast host, Jesse Michels, says that in the 1910s and 1920s the Thule Society, a secretive German occult group tied in the story to the Harz Mountains, held seances and rituals to contact non-human intelligences. According to Michels, the members believed these beings were their ancient ancestors, star beings from the far north beneath the pole star. If true, it would mean the group saw itself as descended from beings from beyond Earth.
thunder-and-lightning-striking-the-spot-: Dennis Asberg, a Swedish treasure hunter whose team says it found a strange object on the Baltic Sea floor in 2011, says odd weather kept happening right over the find. He describes thunder, lightning and other phenomena striking just that spot. He tells it as one of several strange things that, he says, surround the object.
thutmose-iv-s-dream-stela: A researcher named Luke Caverns tells podcast host Jesse Michels about Thutmose IV, a pharaoh, or king, of ancient Egypt. He says that while ruling, Thutmose put up a carved stone tablet now called the Dream Stela, between the paws of the Sphinx, the giant lion statue with a human head at Giza. According to Caverns, the tablet tells how Thutmose, as a boy before he became king, fell asleep in the Sphinx's shade and the Sphinx came to him in a dream.
tibetan-buddhist-dark-retreats: A researcher of the mind and the paranormal, Jeffrey Mishlove, told podcast host Jesse Michels about a Tibetan Buddhist practice called the dark retreat. He says some practitioners go into isolation for a year or more at a time, living in a completely dark cell. He raises it as an example of people seeking unusual states of consciousness.
tic-tac-at-31-times-the-speed-of-sound-w: Deep Prasad, a young researcher interviewed by podcast host Jesse Michels in 2022, talks about the Tic Tac, a white oval object shaped like the mint. He says it is estimated to reach at least 31 times the speed of sound without disturbing the air around it, which would mean it moves in a way no known aircraft can.
tic-tac-encounter-as-testimony-from-reli: A philosopher, James Madden, talking with podcast host Jesse Michels, uses the Tic Tac case as an example: a sighting by Navy pilots of a white oval object, shaped like the mint. He says his evidence for it is the word of seemingly very reliable pilots, naming Alex Dietrich and David Fravor, who have described what they saw. His point is that much of what we know about such encounters rests on trusting credible witnesses.
tic-tac-flir-video-2004: In 2004, off Southern California, a heat-sensing camera on a Navy jet filmed a white oval object shaped like a Tic Tac mint. The camera is called forward-looking infrared, or FLIR. Michels calls it "the famous tic tac video", and he says the thermal image is the best picture of the whole case, which is tied to the aircraft carrier USS Nimitz. A guest named Merrick von Renenamp, retelling what the crews reported, explains how the video came about. After the first jets returned to the carrier, the Navy pilot David Fravor reportedly told another pilot, Chad Underwood, "Hey, we just saw something weird". Underwood then went up and filmed it, and von Renenamp also mentions radar hits. If the video is what they say, it is a recording of the same object the pilots saw with their own eyes.
tic-tac-leaves-as-soon-as-he-heads-for-t: A witness from Skywatcher, a startup that says it tries to call in UFOs, tells podcast host Jesse Michels about a night around February 2025 on a hill at their field site. He says he saw a "tic-tac," a white oval object shaped like the mint, and that as soon as he took about ten steps toward the helicopter, it began to fly away. As he tells it, the object seemed to react to what he was doing.
tic-tac-pilots-names-told-to-bishop-befo: Greg Bishop, a writer on UFOs, says that someone told him the names of the Navy pilots in the 2004 Tic Tac incident, when pilots reported a white oval object shaped like the mint, before those names were public. He names them as David Fravor and Alex Dietrich, and says he was told not to talk about it. He believes it was a test to see whether he would leak secrets.
tic-tac-unloaded-from-a-c-130-in-the-azo: A guest known as UAPGerb, speaking on host Jesse Michels's podcast in 2025, mentions a person stationed with the US Air Force in the Azores, Portuguese islands in the Atlantic. According to UAPGerb, this person claims to have seen a Tic Tac, a white oval object shaped like the mint, unloaded from a C-130, a large military cargo plane, which would mean the military has such an object in hand.
tic-tac-videos-seen-in-the-pentagon-befo: Hal Puthoff, a physicist who has worked on government-funded research into unusual phenomena, says he watched the famous Navy "Tic Tac" videos, footage of a white oval object shaped like the mint, inside the Pentagon before they were made public in 2017. He credits former Pentagon official Lue Elizondo with getting them released, and says other videos exist, some of them better. If true, it would mean the government holds clearer footage than anything the public has seen.
ticom-and-alsos-technology-retrieval-194: A podcast host, Jesse Michels, says that at the end of World War Two, in 1944 and 1945, the Nazis had a great deal of advanced technology in Europe. He names two efforts, TICOM and ALSOS, Allied teams that went in to gather that German technology and know-how. He raises it because, if true, it would show a model for how captured exotic technology could be quietly collected by governments.
tim-burchett-on-the-high-rate-of-researc: A podcast host, Jesse Michels, in an episode about American scientists who have gone missing, cites Tim Burchett, a member of the US Congress. According to Michels, Burchett told the Daily Mail, a British newspaper, that the numbers seem very high in certain areas of research. Michels raises it because, if true, it would point to something unusual happening to people in those fields.
tim-phillips-confirms-borland-s-two-draw: A man named Dylan Borland, speaking on Jesse Michels's podcast, says he made two drawings that ended up with AARO, the Pentagon office that handles reports of unidentified aerial phenomena. Borland says that Tim Phillips, connected to that office, acknowledged that Borland drew the two drawings and that the office was told to classify them under a security classification guide, a rulebook saying which information must be kept secret. If so, it would mean his material was treated as sensitive government information.
tim-phillips-says-triangles-are-real-202: On the podcast of a host named Jesse Michels, a guest named Dylan Borland passes on something he says came from Tim Phillips, a man the story ties to AARO, the Pentagon office that looks into unexplained objects in the sky. According to Borland, sometime in the 2020s Phillips said that triangle-shaped craft are real and that the government wants to know where they come from. If true, it would mean people inside the government accept these triangles as something real and unexplained.
tim-taylor-and-the-adjustment-team: Podcast host Jesse Michels, in an episode about NASA and UFOs, mentions a man named Tim Taylor who told religion scholar Diana Pasulka that he was part of what he called the "adjustment team." Michels relays the claim without spelling out what the team did, but the phrase suggests a hidden group said to change or correct things behind the scenes.
tim-taylor-at-the-anderson-case-dig-this: A guest named Grant Cameron told podcast host Jesse Michels about a 2013 dig tied to something called the Anderson case, where a man named Tim Taylor was pulling material out of the ground. Cameron says a friend told him that when some of the material came up, Taylor said, "This is the real deal." If true, it would suggest the dig turned up something Taylor saw as genuine evidence of a crash.
tim-taylor-converts-to-catholicism-at-th: A podcast host, Jesse Michels, says that a man named Tim Taylor converted to Catholicism right at the Vatican, the home of the Catholic Church in Rome. Michels tells it as a turning point in Taylor's spiritual life.
tim-taylor-disappears-after-15-years-of-: The wife of Charles Hall, a man who says he spent three years with tall white aliens at Area 51, a secret Air Force base in Nevada, speaks of a man named Tim Taylor who had been in touch with the couple for about fifteen years. She says that one day he simply disappeared, and they have never heard from him since.
tim-taylor-helped-linda-brown-write-her-: Chris Bledsoe, a man who says he attracts UFOs and that NASA has studied him, says a man named Tim Taylor helped a woman named Linda Brown write her book in the early 2010s. Bledsoe adds that he has the manuscript, which is about a man named Thomas Townsend Brown, saved on his phone. He tells it to show how closely Taylor was tied to that circle.
tim-taylor-of-aerospace-corporation-take: A podcast host, Jesse Michels, mentions a man named Tim Taylor, who he says works at Aerospace Corporation, a company that does space work for the US government and NASA, the American space agency. Michels says Taylor claims he is taking orders from an angel. If true, it would mean someone inside the space world says he is guided by a non-human being.
tim-taylor-places-piece-of-roswell-crash: Bob McGwier, who calls himself a witness, says that a man named Tim Taylor brought a piece of the Roswell crash, the 1947 event in New Mexico that many say involved an alien craft, and put it in the hands of a North Carolina man, Chris Bledsoe, and others in his family. Bledsoe tells it himself as a test of his family by a man from NASA, the US space agency, who came with a backpack and credentials ranging from Area 51, a secret Air Force test site, to the CIA, the US spy agency, though Bledsoe does not say the metal came from Roswell. Podcast host Jesse Michels adds that Bledsoe somehow knew the material was not from here, which, if true, would hint at a special link between Bledsoe and whatever made it.
tim-taylor-s-background-as-nasa-mission-: A podcast host, Jesse Michels, describes a man named Tim Taylor as a mysterious rocket scientist who, he says, has worked in mission control for NASA, the US space agency, since the 1980s, at Kennedy Space Center in Florida, where NASA launches its rockets. Michels raises it in an episode about why, as its title puts it, NASA studies a man who attracts UFOs. If true, it would mean that someone with strange experiences sits in the heart of the space programme.
tim-taylor-s-downloaded-business-ideas: Podcast host Jesse Michels describes a man named Tim Taylor, who appears in American Cosmic, a book by religion scholar Diana Pasulka. According to Michels, Taylor claims that many of his ideas, including business ideas, came to him as sudden "downloads" from an intelligence he believes is not human. In other episodes Michels speaks of the downloads more generally and adds that Taylor says they came through protocols, or set practices, that he followed. If true, it would mean a non-human mind is feeding ideas to people.
tim-taylor-s-hooded-figure-before-his-in: A UFO researcher named Grant Cameron, on Jesse Michels's podcast, relays what Tim Taylor, a man featured in a book by scholar Diana Pasulka, told him. Cameron says Taylor told him that the night before an invention idea arrived in his head, he woke up to see a hooded figure standing at the end of his bed. The story ties the sudden idea to a visit from some unknown being.
tim-taylor-s-secret-space-program-and-ti: Podcast host Jesse Michels describes Tim Taylor, a man he calls an operative, who appears in American Cosmic, a book by religion scholar Diana Pasulka. According to Michels, the book says Taylor was part of a secret space program involving UFOs, and the story also links him to adjusting timelines. If true, it would mean a hidden government effort working with UFO technology.
tim-taylor-s-sun-gazing-protocols-in-ame: A podcast host, Jesse Michels, says that Tim Taylor, a man he describes as a NASA rocket scientist, talks about his personal routines, which he calls protocols, in American Cosmic, a book by Diana Pasulka. According to Michels, those routines involve being out in the sunlight and looking at the sun. He tells it as a clue to how Taylor says he connects with whatever he experiences.
tim-taylor-says-the-president-handed-him: A man named Chris Bledsoe, whose story of attracting UFOs was the subject of a podcast episode with host Jesse Michels, passes on something he says a man named Tim Taylor told him. According to Bledsoe, Taylor said a president handed him a certain item while they sat together at the dinner table. No date or place is given, but if true it would put the item, and Taylor, very close to the top of government.
tim-taylor-secret-space-program-and-cras: A podcast host, Jesse Michels, retells a story from American Cosmic, a book by the writer Diana Pasulka. In it, a man named Tim Taylor, a NASA mission controller who also works at the Aerospace Corporation, a space research firm, tells her openly that he is part of a secret space program. Michels says Taylor then took her and a Stanford professor, Garry Nolan, to a UFO crash site where they examined material.
tim-taylor-shows-grant-the-jump-room-bui: Grant Cameron, a longtime UFO researcher, says that in 2013 a man named Tim Taylor took him to a former aircraft building that had been turned into offices. He says Taylor told him this was where the "jump room" was, or where its story came from, a term the telling does not explain. Cameron tells it as a glimpse of a secret site tied to Taylor.
tim-taylor-shows-up-with-experiencers-bl: A podcast host, Jesse Michels, says a man named Tim Taylor keeps turning up in the lives of people who report contact with non-human beings. Michels says Taylor appeared in the life of Chris Bledsoe, a man who reports such encounters, and with Charles Hall, who says he lived alongside aliens at Area 51, a secret US military base in Nevada. Michels tells it because, if true, it would suggest one person is quietly following or connecting these witnesses.
tim-taylor-visits-charles-hall: The wife of a man named Charles Hall says that a man called Tim Taylor once came to their home. She tells it on a podcast hosted by Jesse Michels, saying Taylor came because "he found out about Charles". She doesn't say what Taylor wanted, but she tells it as an early sign that someone with outside interest had taken notice of her husband.
tim-taylor-works-for-the-hammer: Bob McGwier, an engineer who says he did contract work for the CIA, the US spy agency, repeats a story about a man named Tim Taylor. He says Taylor works for someone called "the Hammer", and that nobody he knows can say who the Hammer is. A man named Chris Bledsoe, who says he has strange encounters, tells it differently: he says Taylor told him around 2008 to 2011, "I work for the hammer and the hammer works for God," and he links this to The Adjustment Bureau and The Adjustment Team, two stories about hidden agents who quietly steer people's lives, which would suggest an unseen hand behind the whole affair.
time-slows-and-god-speaks-on-the-night-t: A former CIA chief named Rolf Mowatt-Larssen says that at age 40, on a night train from Zurich to Vienna, time seemed to slow down and God was there, aware and standing with him. He says God told him: "do not criticize my church, the old and the new are one." He says he wrote the message down by hand, and he links it to his Bible from West Point, the US Army's military academy.
time-travel-to-14th-century-mount-athos-: Rolf Mowatt-Larssen, a former CIA officer, told the podcast host Jesse Michels that he once travelled back in time. He says that in 1991 he went on a pilgrimage to Mount Athos, a holy mountain in Greece, and dozed off on a stone chair facing a church. As he tells it, he then found himself in the same place centuries earlier, around the 1300s. If it were true, it would mean a person can slip out of their own time and into the past. A second telling on the same show, by a speaker called Ralph, describes seeing the town again in the 1400s or 1500s. In that version he arrived as a monk named Odious Maximus, presented his credentials at the capital, and met figures named the monk Gabriel and Evagrius. The two versions disagree on which century he reached.
time-travelling-nordic-humans-manipulati: Jason Jorjani, a philosopher, says on a podcast that some of the beings people report, tall and Nordic-looking, are in fact humans from the future who achieved time travel somewhere after the year 2050. According to Jorjani, drawing on a work called Closer Encounters, these travellers act across Earth, the Moon and Mars and have been shaping human history. If true, our past would partly be the work of our own descendants.
timothy-leary-supplied-lsd-to-jfk-and-ma: Dan Sheehan, a lawyer, says on a podcast that in the 1960s President John F. Kennedy and Mary Pinchot Meyer, a woman close to him in Washington, took LSD, a mind-altering drug, supplied by Timothy Leary, a psychologist famous for promoting it. Sheehan tells it as part of a wider account of Kennedy's private life and his interest in hidden matters, including UFOs.
timothy-taylor-s-agency-credentials-and-: A podcast host, Jesse Michels, talks about a man named Timothy Taylor, who is linked to NASA and to talk of a possible secret space program. Michels says that, according to Diana Pasulka, a professor who writes about UFO belief, Taylor showed her credentials from several US intelligence agencies. A commentator who goes by UAPGerb says much the same but does not credit Pasulka, and he names access to the NRO, the National Reconnaissance Office, the agency that runs America's spy satellites. If true, it would suggest someone with deep government ties is involved in the subject.
timothy-taylor-s-hierarchy-as-described-: This story is about Timothy Taylor, described as a NASA programme manager long involved in strange and secretive subjects, who was once anonymous and is now fairly well known. According to a guest named Matthew Pines, a religion scholar named Diana Pasulka asked Taylor what the hierarchy is, meaning the ranking of beings, human and non-human. A podcast host, Jesse Michels, repeats it, saying Taylor laid out for Pasulka a hierarchy of beings. Neither gives the full answer here. If true, it would mean someone inside the space agency claims to know an order of intelligent beings above us.
tip-about-a-russian-intelligence-officer: A man called Ralph, described as a former chief at the CIA, the US spy agency, says that in 1991 a Greek man very close to Greece's prime minister gave him a tip. The tip was that a monk at Mount Athos, a Greek mountain full of monasteries, was really a Russian intelligence officer taking on a new identity to go on a spy mission to the United States. Ralph says a file was kept on the monk.
titanic-survivor-s-account-of-angels-in-: Charles Hall, a man who says he spent years with tall white aliens while serving in the Air Force, tells on Jesse Michels's podcast of a book about the Titanic, the ocean liner that sank in the North Atlantic in 1912. Hall says the book describes a survivor, picked up by the rescue ship Carpathia, who reported a group of angels arriving in a craft near the lifeboats and landing on the ledge of an iceberg. Hall tells it as an early sign of such beings, described in the language of the time.
tmbb-spaceships-x-account-suspected-to-b: A podcast host, Jesse Michels, says that after the story of a general named McCasland broke in 2026, people online went hunting for clues about him. According to Michels, the hunt settled on an account called TMBB spaceships on X, the social media site, which some suspected McCasland himself was running. If so, it would be a possible smoking gun, a direct trace of the general speaking about spaceships.
to-the-stars-material-testing-with-milit: A writer named Peter Levenda, billed on a podcast as a CIA historian, told the host Jesse Michels about his time with To the Stars Academy, a private group set up to look into UFOs. He says that around 2019 the group was building ties with US military laboratories to run tests on materials that only those labs could do, and that they felt they were getting close to something. Then, he says, the COVID pandemic hit and the relationship with the military stopped, which matters to him because it would mean serious study of strange materials was cut off just as it began.
told-sensor-research-would-be-career-end: A man named Eric Hazeline, interviewed by the podcast host Jesse Michels, says he began working in his own lab to reproduce some phenomenon and to build a sensor that could detect it. According to him, people in the US intelligence community, the government agencies that gather secret information, warned him that this work would end his career. If true, it would suggest officials were discouraging outside research into the subject.
tom-delonge-books-on-official-and-non-go: Matthew Pines, a researcher and analyst, says on a podcast that the books of Tom DeLonge, a rock musician who later founded a company to study UFOs, point to two kinds of secret UFO work. According to Pines, DeLonge describes official government programs on one side and programs outside the government on the other. If so, it would mean some of this work sits beyond normal public oversight.
tom-delonge-contacts-levenda-to-investig: A writer named Peter Levenda told the podcast host Jesse Michels that a man named Tom DeLonge got in touch with him out of the blue at the end of 2014, by phone and email, to look into UFOs. Levenda tells it as the start of his own involvement in a private effort to investigate the subject.
tom-delonge-email-to-john-podesta-about-: A podcast host, Jesse Michels, says that among the emails of John Podesta, a Washington political figure, which were leaked and published by WikiLeaks, a website that posts leaked documents, there is one from a man named Tom DeLonge with the subject line "General McCasland." According to Michels, DeLonge writes that the general had said he was a skeptic, but he is not, and that DeLonge had been working with him for four months. If true, it would suggest a senior military officer was quietly helping DeLonge around 2015 or 2016.
tom-delonge-narrative-of-a-majestic-styl: Matthew Pines, a researcher and analyst, describes on a podcast what he calls the Tom DeLonge story, after the rock musician who later founded a company to study UFOs. According to Pines, DeLonge's account involves a small controlling group like "Majestic", a name long linked to a supposed secret panel of officials said to oversee the UFO matter. If true, a hidden few would be in charge of the whole subject.
tom-delonge-says-nhi-are-archons: Jesse Michels, a podcast host, says that over breakfast Tom DeLonge, a rock musician who co-founded To the Stars Academy, a company studying UFOs, told him he thought many of the NHI, meaning non-human intelligences, are not friendly. In a later episode, Michels adds that DeLonge framed this through Gnostic thought, an ancient religious tradition, and compared these beings to its archons, ruling powers that hold humans in check. If true, it would mean the visitors are something to be wary of rather than welcomed.
tom-farmer-cia-general-counsel-vetting-p: Harold Malmgren, a former adviser to US presidents, was talking on Jesse Michels' podcast about a man named Tom Farmer, who served as general counsel, meaning top lawyer, for the CIA, America's foreign intelligence agency. Malmgren says Farmer told him he had been involved in Project Paperclip, the US effort after the Second World War to bring German scientists to America, and that his job was checking out those Germans in Germany and Washington. If true, it would put a senior CIA lawyer close to the people and secrets that came over from Germany.
tomb-of-the-birds-and-the-wooden-bird-fo: A researcher named Luke Caverns, talking with podcast host Jesse Michels in 2025, describes a tomb called the Tomb of the Birds in a cliff west of the Great Pyramid at Giza. He tells of a wooden bird said to have been found there during the Second World War, and mentions the television science show Mythbusters in connection with it, suggesting the object may show the ancients knew something about flight.
tomb-of-thutmose-ii-announced-over-a-yea: A researcher named Luke Caverns told podcast host Jesse Michels that when he was in Egypt in October 2024, he heard about the tomb of Thutmose II, an ancient Egyptian king, having already been found earlier that year. His point is that the find was only announced to the public more than a year after it was made, which, if true, would mean big discoveries in Egypt can sit quietly for a long time before anyone is told.
tone-experiments-with-entranced-space-ki: On Jesse Michels' podcast, a researcher whose name is not given described work done in the 1970s at the lab of Andrija Puharich, a researcher who studied psychic abilities and claimed contact with otherworldly beings. The guest says Puharich ran many experiments on children who were put into a trance, for example playing a certain tone and asking them to respond to it, and points to Puharich's recorded session tapes. If true, it would mean these children were being tested as possible channels to something beyond ordinary perception.
tonopah-s4-workers-flown-in-by-janet: A researcher who goes by the online name UAPGerb, speaking on Jesse Michels' podcast, passed on something he learned from a source connected to the Lazy G Ranch in Nevada. He says that workers at an area called S4 on the Tonopah Test Range, a secretive military testing ground in Nevada, must be flown straight there on Janet, the unmarked airline that carries staff to secret Nevada sites, and are not allowed to drive in like other Tonopah employees. If true, it would mean S4 is guarded even more tightly than the rest of an already secret base.
tonopah-test-range-is-literally-area-52: An online UFO researcher who goes by UAPGerb tells podcast host Jesse Michels that the Tonopah Test Range, a military testing area in Nevada, is literally named Area 52. The name plays on Area 51, the famously secret Nevada base, and he offers it as a sign of where hidden work may happen.
tooth-device-demonstration-at-the-pentag: Andrija Puharich, a researcher described in a podcast episode title as a CIA scientist, says in recorded remarks that in the 1960s he and others gave a demonstration at the Pentagon, the headquarters of the US military. According to him, they fitted a small device, worn at the tooth, to a general to show what it could do. He tells it as a sign that the military took his unusual inventions seriously.
top-secret-files-from-the-late-1800s: Steven Greer, a UFO activist who campaigns for government openness, said on Jesse Michels' podcast that a senior CIA source he does not name told him about very old secrets. According to Greer, there are still top secret US government files about UFOs dating from the late 1800s and early 1900s. If true, it would mean the government was watching this subject before airplanes even existed.
topological-physics-held-by-the-governme: Jesse Michels, a podcast host, says that Hal Puthoff, a physicist who has worked on government research into UFOs, told him that topological physics, a branch of physics about the properties of shapes and spaces, might be held in secret by the government and big aerospace companies. In one retelling Michels adds that Puthoff was unsure whether truly fundamental physics was locked up that way, but thought topological physics probably was. If true, it would mean some advanced science is being kept out of public hands.
toronto-cafe-idea-of-borrowing-other-peo: A researcher named Deep Prasad says that in 2018 he was sitting in a café in Toronto, looked around at the people near him, and came up with the idea of borrowing other people's brain power. He tells it on Jesse Michels's podcast, in an episode about the claim that artificial intelligence is alien technology, as the moment his thinking began.
toronto-death-ray-inventor-and-mossad-mi: A researcher named Dave Rossi told podcast host Jesse Michels about a newspaper clipping from Toronto, Canada, from the late 1950s or early 1960s. Rossi says it described a man who claimed to have invented a death ray, and that visitors from Mossad, Israel's intelligence service, went to see him and afterward reported missing time, a stretch of time they could not account for. If true, it would tie a strange invention to an experience often linked with unexplained encounters.
touching-the-reactor-s-repulsive-field-1: Bob Lazar, a man who says he worked in the late 1980s at S4, a secret site in Nevada where he says the US studied craft not made by humans, told the podcast host Jesse Michels about the power source, or reactor, he says he saw there. He says it made a gravity-like field around itself that you could physically push on and feel pushing back. If true, it would mean someone held technology that controls gravity.
toughbook-programs-lured-ufos-and-downed: A podcast host, Jesse Michels, says a leak from an insider revealed what was recorded on certain Toughbooks, tough military-style laptops, from the 2020s. According to Michels, the programmes on them used temporary flight restrictions, rules that close a patch of US airspace to normal planes, to clear the sky, draw UFOs in, and bring them down with EMP weapons, which send out a burst of energy that knocks out electronics. If true, it would mean the US was actively capturing unknown craft.
townsen-brown-at-caltech-in-the-1920s-di: A podcast host, Jesse Michels, says that in the 1920s, a decade before the rocket pioneer Jack Parsons, a man named Thomas Townsend Brown was at Caltech, a science university in Pasadena, California. Michels says Brown had very different ideas for travel into deep space, tied to getting thrust from lopsided electrical parts called capacitors. He tells it because, if true, a path to space without rockets was explored very early.
townsend-brown-and-ning-li-claims-of-wei: A podcast host, Jesse Michels, says that over the last 70 years a number of people have claimed small effects on gravity. He names the inventor Townsend Brown and a scientist named Ning Li at the University of Alabama in Huntsville, who he says reported objects losing a little weight and a kind of shielding from gravity. If true, it would hint that gravity can be controlled.
townsend-brown-and-the-caroline-group: A podcast host, Jesse Michels, says the inventor Townsend Brown came up against something called the Caroline Group. Michels describes it as an international group of industrialists that seems to soak up all the exotic technology. If true, it would mean unusual inventions were being quietly gathered up by private powers.
townsend-brown-and-the-nassau-group: A podcast host, Jesse Michels, says that Townsend Brown, a man whose life is told in a biography called The Man Who Mastered Gravity, spent a great deal of time in Nassau, the capital of the Bahamas. According to Michels, Brown's biographer Paul Schatzkin even coined a name, the Nassau Group, for a secret group that used to meet there, with figures like Eldridge Reeves Johnson and William Stephenson mentioned alongside it. If true, it would point to a private circle working quietly on Brown's ideas away from public view.
townsend-brown-believed-his-work-bore-on: A podcast host, Jesse Michels, says that Thomas Townsend Brown, a researcher who worked with high voltages, believed his work clearly bore on time travel and was obsessed with the subject. Michels adds that Agnew Bahnson, a man who paid for Brown's work, was famous for saying similar things. If true, it would mean their experiments touched on time itself.
townsend-brown-born-in-zanesville-built-: A podcast host, Jesse Michels, says that an inventor named Townsend Brown was born in 1905 in Zanesville, Ohio. According to Michels, old newspaper clippings show Brown building a wireless telegraph, a device that sends messages without wires, at around age 12. He tells it as an early sign of the gifted inventor Brown would become.
townsend-brown-crash-retrievals-and-gree: A podcast host, Jesse Michels, tells a story about a man named Townsend Brown. Michels says that in the late 1950s and early 1960s Brown would go out into the field in the United States, show official credentials, and recover crashed objects, what people in this world call crash retrievals. According to Michels, Brown found a "green fireball", a glowing green ball of light, that was losing mass, and it was apparently made of barium titanate, a ceramic compound, which would suggest hidden recoveries of unknown material if true.
townsend-brown-fired-by-the-navy-moves-t: A podcast host, Jesse Michels, says that in 1942 the US Navy fired the inventor Townsend Brown without giving a reason. Michels says Brown then mysteriously turned up at the Martin Vega Corporation, an aircraft company, a year before Skunk Works, a famous secret aircraft design unit, was formed. He tells it because, if true, Brown's work may have quietly fed into secret aircraft projects.
townsend-brown-in-the-bahamas-with-willi: Podcast host Jesse Michels, in a 2025 episode, talks about a man named Townsend Brown. Michels says Brown spent an unusual amount of time in the Bahamas with William Stephenson, a spy for Winston Churchill who inspired the character James Bond, which would tie Brown to the world of intelligence agencies.
townsend-brown-parachutes-into-germany-t: On his podcast, the host Jesse Michels tells a story about Townsend Brown, an American inventor who tried to move objects using electricity in place of ordinary thrust. Michels says that in 1944 Brown parachuted behind enemy lines into Germany to look into a German UFO program and the Foo Fighters, the glowing balls of light that wartime pilots reported following their planes. He points to a biography of Brown, The Man Who Mastered Gravity by Paul Schatzkin, and links the mission to the wartime spy chiefs Bill Donovan and William Stephenson, and if true it would mean the Allies took German flying-object reports seriously enough to send a scientist in.
townsend-brown-possibly-involved-in-a-cr: A podcast host, Jesse Michels, says he has some evidence that the inventor Townsend Brown may have taken part in recovering a crashed UFO in the United States. If true, it would tie a known inventor of unusual propulsion to hidden non-human craft.
townsend-brown-s-1960s-work-northrop-b-2: A podcast host, Jesse Michels, says that an American inventor named Townsend Brown ran experiments in the 1960s, shortly before his work was quietly handed over to Northrop Grumman, a big aircraft maker, for the B-2, a US bomber plane. Michels adds that Brown also gave a presentation to the RAND Corporation, a research group that advises the US military. If that's right, it would mean Brown's private research ended up inside secret military aircraft projects.
townsend-brown-s-anti-gravity-success-in: A podcast host, Jesse Michels, says that an American inventor named Townsend Brown finally got a positive result from his anti-gravity experiments, meaning attempts to make objects push against gravity, while working in Paris in the 1950s. According to Michels, when Brown flew back to the United States he was picked up in a big Cadillac by Robert Sarbacher, a scientist who advised the US government. The story suggests that people close to government took a quiet interest in Brown's work.
townsend-brown-s-electrogravitics-experi: Steven Greer, a UFO activist, says on Jesse Michels' podcast that in the late 1920s the inventor Townsend Brown was already experimenting with electrogravitics, the idea that strong electric charges can produce a force that works against gravity. Greer says the work used very high voltage at low power, tuned to certain resonant frequencies, and he cites his own Disclosure Project collection of intelligence material. If true, it would mean the roots of anti-gravity research go back almost a century.
townsend-brown-s-experiments-in-oil: A guest named Charles, on podcast host Jesse Michels's show, tells of Townsend Brown, an American inventor linked to ideas about antigravity propulsion, meaning a way to move craft without ordinary thrust. Charles says Brown did some of his experiments in oil. If his work held up, it would hint at a new way to fly.
townsend-brown-s-gravitational-anomaly-e: A podcast host, Jesse Michels, says that an American inventor named Townsend Brown spent a lot of time in Nassau, the capital of the Bahamas. According to Michels, Brown went on expeditions there to look for gravitational anomalies, meaning places where gravity seems to behave oddly. If true, it would show Brown searching the natural world for clues to his ideas about gravity.
townsend-brown-s-gravitator-was-a-time-m: A podcast host, Jesse Michels, has talked in several episodes about T. Townsend Brown, an American inventor of the mid-1900s who built a device he called a gravitator, meant to tie electricity and magnetism to gravity. Citing a biography of Brown called The Man Who Mastered Gravity, Michels says a man named Morgan once blew up and called the device a time machine. In other episodes Michels says Brown made more progress than anyone knew, was privately obsessed with time travel, and even called himself a time traveler, and he credits Brown's daughter as a source for that, which would make Brown's work much more than an odd engine.
townsend-brown-s-shortwave-contact-with-: A podcast host, Jesse Michels, says that an American inventor named Townsend Brown often talked about 'space brothers', friendly aliens, and about communicating with them. In a later episode Michels credits this to Agnew Bahnson, a businessman who worked with Brown, and says Brown claimed to be in touch with aliens 'half the time'. If true, it would mean a serious inventor believed he had a line to beings from elsewhere.
townsend-brown-s-time-travel-tech-taken-: Podcast host Jesse Michels says that an inventor named Townsend Brown kept saying his time travel technology had been taken by a group in Nassau, in the Bahamas. Michels draws this from Paul Schatzkin, author of a book about Brown called The Man Who Mastered Gravity, and from Brown's daughter. If true, it would mean someone quietly took over technology that Brown believed could move through time.
townsend-brown-s-ufo-interaction-at-age-: The podcast host Jesse Michels has told several times how the inventor Townsend Brown, who worked on electric anti-gravity ideas, had a UFO experience around 1922 at about age 17, possibly on Catalina Island off California, where he says a small orb of light came right up to him. Michels says that, according to Brown's daughter, this was when Brown 'downloaded his life's work', at a time when he had a lab in Pasadena, though once he hedges on the age and the place. If true, it would mean one of the pioneers of anti-gravity research got his ideas from a close encounter.
townsend-brown-takes-crash-material-from: A podcast host, Jesse Michels, says that in the late 1950s the inventor Townsend Brown walked into Harvard, showed his credentials, and walked out with material said to come from a crashed craft. In another telling Michels puts it in 1958 in Hartford, Connecticut, says the historian Michael Swords documented it, and ties it to the astronomer J. Allen Hynek, to a sky-watching effort called Project Moon Watch, and to Blue Book, the US Air Force's UFO study of the 1950s and 60s. If true, it would mean someone with official backing was quietly collecting crash material back then.
townsend-brown-workbooks-posted-online-2: Harold Malmgren, a former adviser to US presidents, mentioned on Jesse Michels' podcast in 2025 that someone had just posted on the internet the workbooks of Townsend Brown, an inventor who worked on electric anti-gravity ideas. If so, it would put a pioneer's private research notes in front of the public.
townsend-brown-worse-than-a-thermonuclea: A podcast host, Jesse Michels, quotes a line from The Man Who Mastered Gravity, a biography of an inventor named Townsend Brown written by Paul Schatzkin. According to Michels, the book says that something tied to Brown's work would make a thermonuclear bomb, the most powerful kind of nuclear weapon, look like a child's firecracker. He tells it to show how much power, if true, that work was thought to hold.
townsend-s-repelling-bismuth-raised-at-m: The podcast host Jesse Michels points to an interview the physicist Louis Witten gave to the American Institute of Physics, a professional body that records scientists' life stories. Michels says that in it Witten recalls a man named Townsend, linked to the aerospace firm Martin and its research institute known as RIAS in the 1950s, who claimed to have a form of bismuth, a heavy metal, that pushed away instead of pulling. If true, it would mean a defense company heard claims of a material that behaves against normal gravity.
townspeople-claim-1992-ufo-crash-recover: The podcast host Jesse Michels says that in 1992 many people living near Brookhaven National Laboratory, a government science lab on Long Island, New York, said a UFO crashed and the lab collected it. In other retellings he dates it only to the 1990s and points to a sheriff's account, or names the town as South Haven and says everybody there saw the lab take the craft inside. If true, it would mean a national lab recovered a crashed craft in front of local witnesses.
trace-relation-proven-to-be-a-partial-or: A researcher named Don Hoffman, whom a podcast title calls an MIT scientist, says that about two years before the interview he suspected a piece of his mathematical theory, a link he calls the trace relation, was a partial order, a precise kind of mathematical ranking. He says he took it to a colleague, Jayton Posash, who called it too pretty to be true, then checked it while at Heathrow airport in London and proved it. Hoffman tells it because it would mean the math behind his ideas about reality holds up.
training-army-intelligence-officers-in-r: A researcher named Hal Puthoff, described in a podcast title as a CIA UFO expert, says he once stopped other work because he was busy almost around the clock training US Army intelligence officers. The training was in remote viewing, the practice of trying to perceive distant places or things using only the mind. If true, it would mean the army took such abilities seriously enough to teach them.
training-children-in-extraocular-vision-: A scientist named Rupert Sheldrake told podcast host Jesse Michels that groups in Mexico and Spain are training children in extraocular vision, which means seeing without using the eyes. He says he knows about the work in Spain through a colleague there who is doing it, and he is not sure whether anything like it is happening in the US or Britain. If true, it would suggest this ability can be taught.
training-instructor-s-account-of-ghosts-: Charles Hall says he worked as a weather observer at Nellis Air Force Base in Nevada around 1964 and 1965, and he wrote about it in his book Millennial Hospitality. On Jesse Michels's podcast he says that the airman training him told him about "ghosts" using the restroom in the old weather station. Hall says those ghosts were really a group of five tall white aliens who had come in off the runway, which would mean the base staff knew about the visitors and had a polite word for them.
transcript-of-brad-sorensen-arvs-built-l: Steven Greer, a doctor who campaigns for government disclosure of UFO secrets, says he has a full transcript of a man named Brad Sorensen talking to an aerospace writer. In it, Greer says, Sorensen describes "ARVs", alien reproduction vehicles, meaning human-built craft copied from alien ones, being built since the late 1950s, and seeing them at Norton Air Force Base in California in 1988. A researcher who goes by UAPGerb points to what seems the same file, posted online as a Norton base internal document dated 1990 and naming the writer as Bill Scott.
transfer-of-ufo-material-from-lockheed-m: A podcast host, Jesse Michels, says that UFO material held by Lockheed Martin, a major US defence company, was moved to Bigelow Aerospace, a private space company in Las Vegas owned by Bob Bigelow, through a special access program, a tightly restricted secret government project. In one telling, Michels says the plan came from Dr. James Ryder, a Lockheed vice president who has since died, and that it shaped OSAP, a Pentagon-funded study of unexplained aerial reports. In another he puts it next to Kona Blue, a programme he also counts as a real UFO programme. If true, it would mean a defence company held recovered UFO material and passed it on to a private firm.
transistor-patents-traced-to-1930s-germa: A podcast host, Jesse Michels, says in passing that the patents for the transistor, the tiny switch at the heart of all modern electronics, have been traced back to Germany in the 1930s. He raises it in an episode about the idea that artificial intelligence is alien technology, so the point, if true, would be that the roots of our computing age are older and stranger than the usual history says.
translucent-acorn-shaped-craft-over-fish: A man named Tim Alberino, who went to the Alto Nanay region of the Amazon in Peru around 2023, told podcast host Jesse Michels what a local fisherman described to him, drawing it on a clear plastic chalkboard. According to Alberino, the man said he was pulling up his nets at night when suddenly it was as if someone turned the lights on or the sun came up, and he looked up to see a see-through, acorn-shaped craft 30 or 40 feet above him. If true, it would be a close sighting of an unknown craft by an ordinary local witness.
travis-taylor-arrives-as-a-skeptic: The owner of Skinwalker Ranch, a property in Utah where people report strange happenings, says a scientist named Dr. Travis Taylor flew out to the ranch with him for the first time as "an absolute skeptic". He tells it on Jesse Michels's podcast to show that even a doubter on his team started out unconvinced, which would make what Taylor later saw there count for more.
travis-taylor-zapped-at-skinwalker-ranch: Skinwalker Ranch is a property in Utah with a long reputation for strange happenings, and a researcher named Grant Cameron tells a story about it on the podcast of host Jesse Michels. Cameron says that sometime in the 2020s a man there named Travis Taylor was "mouthing off" and was given "a little zap" involving radioactivity, without saying who or what did it. People tell it because, if true, it would suggest that something at the ranch reacts to the people studying it.
travis-walton-abduction-1975: A documentary filmmaker, James Fox, tells podcast host Jesse Michels about Travis Walton, a man who says he was taken by a UFO in 1975. Fox says it happened in a very remote mountain area near Snowflake, Arizona. If true, it would be one of the best-known cases of a person taken aboard a craft.
